title: Data — Where It Lives and What It Proves

lessons.title: What counts as data, and what is just noise with confidence
paragraphs: Good to see you. Today AI and Computing earns its keep. I am Professor Juhani Korhonen, and this is Data — Where It Lives and What It Proves. This is lesson one of six: what counts as data, and what is just noise with confidence. I will write the units on the board before opinions, every time. That is my habit, and it will be yours by the end of this class. Bring your curiosity, a pencil, and a healthy suspicion of round confident numbers; the rest is provided.

Here is what this lesson teaches, plainly. First, what data is: recorded observations, written down in a form you can check later. Second, what data is not: a feeling, a rumour, a confident sentence, or a number somebody invented because a number was needed. Third, how to tell the difference, using three questions you can ask about anything anyone shows you. By the end you will be able to look at a claim and say, calmly and correctly, whether there is data under it or only confidence on top of it. That is worth knowing, because most bad decisions begin with someone mistaking confidence for evidence.

Let us start with a definition. A definition is a sentence that tells you what a word means and what it does not mean. Data means recorded observations. Each word matters. An observation is something noticed through the senses or through an instrument: you saw it, you heard it, you counted it, a sensor measured it. Recorded means it was written down, saved, or stored somewhere outside a person's memory, so it can be checked later by someone else. Data is the plural of datum, which is Latin for a thing given. One recorded observation is a datum. Several of them, gathered together, are data. In ordinary speech people say data is, even though the word is plural. I will not correct you for that. I will correct you for calling an opinion data. That error costs money.

Consider a small marketing business, because we will use one throughout this class. Imagine a company with a customer list, a website, and a modest budget for advertisements. The owner says, our customers love the new service. That sentence may be true. It is not data. It is a claim. A claim is a statement offered as true, whether or not anyone has checked it. Now suppose the owner shows you a list: forty-two customers were emailed last Tuesday, thirty-one opened the message, and nine booked a call. Those are recorded observations. Someone counted. The counts were written down. You can check them against the email system. That is data. Notice the difference. The first sentence feels warm. The second one can be verified. Warmth is not verification.

Here is the first test, and I want you to hold onto it. Data can be checked by someone who was not there. If the only way to know a thing is to trust the person saying it, you do not have data. You have testimony. Testimony means a person's report of what they believe happened. Testimony is not worthless. Witnesses matter in courts and in life. But testimony depends on memory, and memory is a poor storage device. Memory edits. Memory forgets the inconvenient parts and sharpens the flattering parts, usually without asking permission. A record does not do that. A record written on Tuesday still says on Friday what it said on Tuesday. That is the entire advantage, and it is a large one.

Now the opposite of data in this lesson is not falsehood. The opposite is noise with confidence. Noise, in this class, means random variation: the ups and downs that happen for no meaningful reason. If you flip a fair coin ten times, you might get seven heads. Nothing caused the seven. The coin has no preference. The seven is noise. Confidence means sounding certain. Noise with confidence is a random result described as if it were a discovery. It is the most common substance in business meetings, and I say that without exaggeration, which you will learn is a high standard for me.

Let me give you a small honest example with numbers, because numbers are where this lesson lives. Our marketing business runs an advertisement for five days. On Monday, one hundred people see the advertisement and four of them click it. On Tuesday, one hundred people see it and six click. On Wednesday, one hundred people see it and three click. The owner announces on Wednesday evening that interest is collapsing and the advertisement must be replaced. Is that data speaking? The counts are data, yes. They were recorded. But the conclusion is noise with confidence. With numbers this small, a difference between six clicks and three clicks is well inside ordinary random variation. If nothing at all had changed, you would still expect days like Tuesday and days like Wednesday, simply because small counts jump around. A count of three and a count of six, out of one hundred, do not prove a trend. They prove that counting happened. That distinction — between the count, which is real, and the story pasted onto the count, which may not be — is the heart of this lesson.

So if X is a small count, then Y, a large conclusion, does not follow. Hold onto that. Small numbers swing widely. Large numbers settle down. We will do the arithmetic properly in lesson three, when we study samples. For now, remember the shape of the error: a true count, an untrue certainty.

Next, a word you will meet everywhere: a metric. A metric is a number chosen to stand for something you care about. Clicks are a metric for interest. Revenue is a metric for sales. Neither one is the thing itself. Interest is a state of mind. A click is a finger pressing a button, which usually means interest and sometimes means an accident. When someone shows you a metric, ask what it stands for and what it leaves out. A business can double its clicks while halving its sales, if the new advertisement attracts curious people who never buy. The metric rose. The business fell. Both statements are true, and only one of them matters. Choosing a metric is a decision, not a discovery, and decisions can be wrong.

Now let me teach you the three questions. When anyone — a colleague, a salesperson, a headline, or your own hopeful brain — presents you with a finding, ask these. Question one: what exactly was observed? Not what was concluded. What was observed. Question two: how many observations are there? Question three: where is the record, and can I see all of it, not only the part being shown to me? Three questions. They take twenty seconds. They will save you, over a lifetime, a sum I will not estimate, because I do not invent numbers. I only note that the sum is not small.

Apply them to our owner. A consultant tells him: businesses like yours typically see a forty percent lift from this tool. Question one: what was observed? The consultant does not say. Question two: how many businesses? The consultant says, many. Many is not a number. Question three: where is the record? There is a brochure. A brochure is not a record. It is an advertisement for the claim. Verdict: there may be data somewhere behind that sentence, but none of it has been shown to you, so for you, today, it is confidence without data. You may still buy the tool. People buy things for many reasons. But do not tell yourself the evidence persuaded you. It did not. It was not present.

Contrast that with an honest record from the same business. The business keeps a predictions record. Each week it writes down, in advance, what it expects to happen — for example, how many enquiries a campaign will produce — and later it writes down what actually happened, hits and misses printed together, at the same size, in the same list. That is data honesty, and it deserves the name. The misses are not hidden in a drawer. The hits are not enlarged. Because the predictions were recorded before the outcomes were known, nobody could quietly rewrite them afterwards. A record made in advance, kept whole, is the strongest kind of everyday data a small business can own. We will return to this example in lesson six, because it shows what data can prove and what it cannot.

Notice what made that record strong. It was not cleverness. It was timing and completeness. Timing: the observation was written before the result. Completeness: all of it was kept, the flattering and the unflattering together. A record that keeps only successes is not a record of performance. It is a record of successes. Those are different objects, and confusing them is how businesses lie to themselves without ever saying a false word. Every individual entry can be accurate while the collection misleads. Remember that sentence. It will matter again when we reach charts in lesson five.

Let us define two more terms while we are here, because sloppy words make sloppy data. A fact is a statement that is true and can be shown to be true. An anecdote is a single story about a single case. Anecdotes are observations, in a weak sense — something did happen to someone — but one case cannot tell you what usually happens. If one customer writes to say the service changed his life, that is one datum about one customer. It tells you nothing reliable about the other nine hundred and ninety-nine. The plural of anecdote is not data. Actually, a pile of anecdotes, collected carelessly, is worse than one anecdote, because the pile looks like evidence while remaining a pile of stories. Data begins when cases are collected by a rule, not by enthusiasm. Collected by a rule means: you decided in advance which cases count, and you took all of them, not only the ones that pleased you.

Here is a quieter example. The business keeps a customer list with names, email addresses, and the date each person first bought something. Is that data? Yes. Each entry is a recorded observation: this person, this address, this date. Is the list good data? That is a different question, and a better one. If addresses were typed in haste, some will be wrong. If customers who asked to be removed are still on it, the list is out of date. Data can be real and still be poor. Poor data is recorded observation with errors, gaps, or staleness in it. The opposite error of this lesson also exists: dismissing real data because it is imperfect. Imperfect data, used with its flaws stated, beats confident guessing. Perfect data does not exist outside of textbooks, and I include my own textbooks in that remark.

Let me pause and give you the guided moment for this lesson. This is the doing part. Think of the most recent claim someone made to you with a number in it. It might be at work. It might be in an advertisement. It might be your own claim, which is the hardest kind to examine and therefore the most valuable. Now run the three questions on it, slowly. What exactly was observed? If you cannot answer, say so out loud: I do not know what was observed. How many observations were there? If the answer is a word like many, or typical, or everyone, notice that no number was given. Where is the record, and can you see all of it? Picture the actual record — a list, a log, a file — or notice that you are picturing nothing. Done. You have just performed the basic move of this entire class. It took less than a minute. Do it often enough and it becomes reflex, which is where I want it.

One more distinction before the recap, because it causes endless confusion. Precision is not accuracy. Precision means the number is stated in fine detail. Accuracy means the number is close to the truth. A report that says sales rose by thirty-seven point four percent sounds precise. If the underlying count was taken from a broken till and half the receipts were missing, the number is precise and wrong. Detail is cheap. Anyone can add a decimal point. Accuracy is expensive, because it requires careful counting. When a number arrives wearing a decimal point, do not be impressed. Ask how it was counted. A whole number honestly counted outranks a decimal invented to impress, every time.

And the mirror image: a vague statement can be accurate. Saying about a third of our customers return within a month may be exactly right, if someone counted returning customers, counted all customers, and divided. We will learn to do that division properly in lesson two. The point for today is that the sound of a claim — crisp or vague, confident or hesitant — carries no information about whether data stands under it. Only the record carries that information. Judge the record. Ignore the tone. Tone is weather. Records are climate.

Let me also say what data cannot do, because this lesson is titled what counts as data, and honest teaching includes limits. Data cannot tell you what to want. It cannot tell the owner whether to chase growth or stability, whether to be kind or merely legal. Data describes what was observed. Decisions require values as well as observations. A person who says the data made me do it is usually hiding a choice they made themselves. Data informs choices. It does not make them, and it does not excuse them. Keep that fence standing and you will reason better than most professionals I have met.

Now a companion word to noise: signal. A signal is a real pattern — a difference or a change that is actually there, caused by something, and large enough to stand above the noise. If our business sends two different email subject lines, each to five thousand customers, and one produces four hundred replies while the other produces two hundred, that gap is probably signal. Five thousand is a large count. Large counts settle, as I said. If instead each subject line went to fifty customers, and one produced four replies and the other produced two, that gap is probably noise wearing a suit. Same ratio — double — completely different meaning, because the counts underneath differ. This is why question two, how many observations, is not pedantry. It is the difference between learning something and fooling yourself at speed. Whenever someone reports a percentage, demand the count underneath it. A percentage without a count is a hat without a head. Fifty percent of two is one. Fifty percent of two thousand is one thousand. The percentage is identical. The evidence is not.

A related trap deserves its own paragraph: the missing denominator. A denominator is the bottom number in a fraction — the total out of which the top number came. Nine customers complained this week. Is that bad? You cannot know until you know the denominator. Nine complaints out of ten customers is a catastrophe. Nine complaints out of nine thousand customers is a quiet week. People who wish to alarm you will give you the top number alone. People who wish to soothe you will do the same, in the other direction. The honest habit is mechanical: every time you hear a count of something interesting, ask, out of how many. Make it a reflex, like checking a mirror before changing lanes. Lesson five will show you charts built entirely on hiding denominators. You will be ready for them.

Another quiet failure: survivorship. Survivorship bias means you only see the cases that survived some process, and the missing cases would have changed the picture. Our business interviews its ten happiest long-term customers and concludes that customers stay because of friendly service. Perhaps. But the customers who left — the ones who did not survive as customers — were not interviewed, and they might have left precisely because of the service. The record of current customers is real data about current customers. It is silent about the departed, and conclusions about why people stay, drawn only from people who stayed, are built on that silence. Whenever a collection is shown to you, ask who is missing from it and why. A collection with a hole in it is still data, but only about what is inside the hole's border.

Let me also distinguish measurement from counting, because both produce data and they fail differently. Counting is deciding how many: how many orders, how many visitors, how many complaints. Counting fails when the rule for what counts is fuzzy. Does a visitor who opens the page twice count once or twice? Either rule can be defended. Switching rules halfway through the month cannot. Measurement is deciding how much: how long a call lasted, how heavy a parcel is, how satisfied a customer says they are on a scale from one to five. Measurement fails when the instrument is off — a clock running fast, a scale uncalibrated, a survey question worded to push the answer. When you inspect a record, ask which kind it is, counting or measuring, and then ask how the counting rule or the instrument could have gone wrong. You will not always find an error. You will always learn how much trust the record has earned.

Satisfaction scores deserve thirty seconds of their own, because businesses love them and they are the softest data in this lesson. A customer circling four out of five has recorded something — a mark on a form — but what it stands for is murky. One customer's four is another customer's five. Some customers never give the top mark on principle. Others give it to end the conversation. Treat such scores as weak data: real records, loosely connected to the thing they claim to measure. They are not useless. A fall from four point six to three point nine across thousands of replies probably signals something real. A difference between four point one and four point two across forty replies signals nothing except that forty people filled in a form. Size again. It always comes back to size, and to whether the record was kept whole.

One more example from our business, this time about money, because money concentrates the mind. The owner says advertising works because revenue rose in the month after the campaign began. The revenue figures are data — recorded, checkable, from the till and the bank. But two true facts side by side do not yet make a proof. Revenue also rises in December for reasons that have nothing to do with advertising, and falls in January for the same reason. That problem — things moving together — is lesson four, correlation and causation, and we will take it apart properly there. For today, file the shape of it: data can be genuine, relevant, and still insufficient for the conclusion being drawn from it. Insufficient is not the same as worthless. It means the honest sentence is we do not know yet, and that sentence, spoken plainly, is a sign of a well-run mind, not a weak one.

I will add one practical habit before the recap, because habits outlast lectures. Keep a small notebook, or a file, for claims. When someone gives you a number that matters — a promised lift, a forecast, a typical result — write it down with the date and the name of the person who said it. In a month, compare the record with what happened. This is the predictions-record idea from earlier, applied to other people's confidence. You will discover, within a few months, whose confidence is calibrated — whose seventy percent means roughly seventy percent — and whose confidence is decoration. That discovery is data about people, collected by a rule, kept whole. It will quietly improve every decision you make afterwards. No software required. A pencil will do, although lesson two will offer you a better tool.

Two more terms, briefly, because you will hear them used loosely and I prefer them used exactly. Primary data is data you collected yourself, for your own question, by your own rule. The customer list our business maintains is primary data. Secondary data is data someone else collected, for their question, which you are borrowing for yours. Industry averages are secondary data. Secondary data is not inferior by definition — a national statistics office counts better than you do — but it was collected under someone else's rule, for someone else's purpose, and the fit to your question is your problem to check. When the consultant says businesses like yours, the words like yours are doing heavy lifting. Like yours in size? In country? In what they sell? Each answer changes whether the borrowed data describes you at all. Ask. The asking is free.

And now the hardest case, which I save for near the end because it involves you. Your own memory of your own business is the data source you will trust most and should trust least. The owner remembers the campaign that worked. He remembers the delighted customer. The failed campaign and the angry customer fade, not from dishonesty but from ordinary human storage. This is why the record must live outside the head. Write it down at the time, all of it, by a rule. Future you is a stranger. Leave that stranger good records. I have kept laboratory notebooks for decades, and the notebook has corrected my memory more times than my memory has corrected the notebook. The count is not close.

So the standard for this class is now set, and it is not a high bar dressed as one. It is a low bar, honestly cleared: observe, record, keep it whole, state the count, name the denominator, and let the conclusion be exactly as large as the record allows — no larger. Most of what calls itself data-driven fails that bar. You, after one lesson, already know how to check. That is a good return on thirty minutes.

One last worked check, start to finish, so you see the whole method on one claim. A software seller tells our owner that his tool finds, on average, twenty percent more repeat customers. Run the questions. What was observed? After pressing, the seller says repeat purchases were counted in the shops using the tool. How many observations? He says the figure comes from twelve shops over one spring. Where is the record? He cannot show it; it belongs to his company. Now judge precisely. Twelve shops is a real count, not a fog. One spring is a real period. But you cannot see the record, you do not know how repeat was defined, and you do not know whether the twelve shops were chosen because their numbers pleased the seller. The correct verdict is not liar. The correct verdict is unverified: a claim with a shape of data behind it that has not been shown. Unverified claims may turn out true. You simply may not spend as if they already have. That sentence — unverified, not false — is the exact, dry judgement this lesson exists to teach. Most claims you meet will land there, and landing there honestly is a success, not a failure of nerve.

Recap, in order. One: data is recorded observation — noticed, counted or measured, and written down where others can check it. Two: a claim without a checkable record is confidence, not evidence, however warmly it is delivered. Three: noise is random variation, and small counts swing widely, so a small count cannot carry a large conclusion. Four: a metric is a number chosen to stand for something else; ask what it stands for and what it leaves out. Five: ask the three questions — what was observed, how many observations, and where is the whole record. Six: a record made in advance and kept whole, hits and misses together, is data at its most honest. Seven: precision is not accuracy, and tone is not evidence.

Before you go, one sentence to carry into every meeting you attend this year. When the room goes quiet after a confident number, you are allowed to be the person who asks, politely, what was counted, how many there were, and where the record is. You will occasionally be unpopular for eleven seconds. Then the room will think more clearly, which is the entire point.

Next, you will answer questions on this lesson — ten or so, about what I actually taught here and nothing else. The full text of this lesson stays open beside the questions. Going back to read is learning, not cheating. Use it. Write the three questions somewhere you will see them. Paper is fine. Paper has an excellent record of surviving, which is more than can be said for most confident claims made in warm rooms by people holding brochures instead of records.
In lesson two we take the records themselves apart: tables, rows, columns, and the humble spreadsheet, which is a better invention than it gets credit for. Bring your curiosity; the rest is provided.

lessons.title: Tables, records, and the humble spreadsheet
paragraphs: Good to see you. Today AI and Computing earns its keep. I am Professor Juhani Korhonen, and this is lesson two of six in Data — Where It Lives and What It Proves: tables, records, and the humble spreadsheet. In lesson one we established what data is: recorded observations, kept whole, that someone else can check. Today we look at where those records actually live, and at the shape that makes them useful instead of merely stored. I write the units on the board before opinions, every time. The unit on the board today is structure. Bring your curiosity, and if you have a messy list of your own somewhere, bring that too — by the end of the hour it will have rows, columns, and no excuses; the rest is provided.

A table is data arranged in rows and columns. That is the whole definition, and it is enough. A row is one horizontal line: one case, one person, one order, one day — one thing, with its facts beside it. A column is one vertical line: one kind of fact, recorded the same way for every row. In our small marketing business, the customer list is a table. Each row is one customer. The columns are name, email address, the date the person first bought, and what they bought. Four columns. Perhaps eight hundred rows. Nothing about this is glamorous, and everything about this class depends on it, because a table with honest rows and consistent columns can answer questions. A pile of notes cannot, or not without a weekend of archaeology first.

The single most important rule of tables is this: one row, one thing. If a row is a customer, every row is a customer — not a customer, then an order, then a note about a phone call, all mixed in one list. Mixing kinds of things in one table is the original sin of small-business data. It feels harmless while you type. It becomes expensive the first time you ask the table a question, because the table can no longer tell you what its rows mean. The second rule follows: one column, one kind of fact, in one format. If the date column holds dates, it holds dates — the same style of date, every row. The day a column starts holding dates in one row, amounts of money in another, and the word soon in a third, it stops being a column and becomes a drawer. Drawers are for socks. Data belongs in columns.

A record is one complete row: all the facts you keep about one case. A field is one cell: the single fact where a row and a column meet — this customer's email address, that order's date. These three words — record, field, table — are the entire vocabulary of this lesson's first half, and they are worth having exactly. When a colleague says the data is a mess, they usually mean one of three precise things: records are missing, fields are inconsistent, or two tables that should agree do not. Naming which one it is turns a complaint into a task. Tasks can be finished. Complaints cannot.

Now, the humble spreadsheet. A spreadsheet is a program that holds a table and does arithmetic on it: adding columns, sorting rows, filtering to the rows that match a condition, and computing totals, averages, and percentages. It is humble because it sits on nearly every computer, costs little or nothing, and excites nobody. It is also, used honestly, the most powerful data tool a small business owns. Databases and dashboards exist, and we will speak of them shortly, but the spreadsheet is where understanding starts, because in a spreadsheet you can see the rows. Seeing the rows is a virtue. Systems that hide the rows from you also hide the errors from you, and errors prefer privacy.

Let us do real work. Our business wants to know what share of its customers come back for a second purchase. In the spreadsheet, the customer table has eight hundred rows — eight hundred customers. A column marks whether each customer bought a second time: yes or no. Count the yes rows: two hundred and forty. Now the arithmetic, done slowly, because this is the calculation half the business world gets quietly wrong. A proportion is the part divided by the whole. Two hundred and forty divided by eight hundred is zero point three. A percentage is a proportion multiplied by one hundred. Zero point three times one hundred is thirty. So thirty percent of customers bought a second time. The denominator — the whole — is eight hundred, stated out loud, as lesson one taught you. If anyone reports that figure as repeat business is thirty percent without the eight hundred standing next to it, send them back to lesson one. I will wait.

Sorting and filtering are the two moves you will use daily. Sorting means rearranging rows by one column: customers by date, orders by size, complaints by day of the week. Sorting is how patterns become visible — the ten largest orders at the top of the list tell a story that the same orders scattered through eight hundred rows do not. Filtering means showing only the rows that meet a condition: only customers from one town, only orders from March, only the predictions record rows marked miss. Filtering is how you ask a table a narrower question. Notice that filtering does not delete. The hidden rows still exist. The moment a filter starts being treated as the whole table, you have built yourself a survivorship trap of the kind lesson one described — you are studying the cases that passed your filter and forgetting the rest exist. Filters are lenses, not editors.

Totals and averages come next, and averages need care. An average, in this class, means the mean unless I say otherwise: add all the values, divide by how many values there are. Our business sold five orders on Monday: ten dollars, twenty dollars, thirty dollars, forty dollars, and one hundred dollars. The total is two hundred dollars. The count is five. Two hundred divided by five is forty. The average order is forty dollars. True, and quietly misleading, because four of the five orders were below it. One large order pulled the average upward like a magnet. For such data there is a second summary: the median, which is the middle value when the values are lined up in order. Line them up: ten, twenty, thirty, forty, one hundred. The middle one is thirty. The median order is thirty dollars. Neither number lies. They answer different questions. The mean tells you where the money is. The median tells you what a typical order looks like. A report that gives you only the mean, for data with a few very large values in it, is leaning — politely, arithmetically, but leaning. Lesson five will deal with leaning in full. For now, when values vary wildly, ask for both numbers. Two numbers, honestly given, are harder to lean with than one.

Now the unglamorous half of the lesson, which is the half that determines whether any of this works: keeping the table clean. Four diseases afflict every real table, and I will name them exactly. Duplicates: the same customer entered twice, perhaps once as Robert Smith and once as Bob Smith, so your eight hundred customers are really seven hundred and sixty people and forty ghosts. Ghosts receive mail, inflate counts, and make percentages wrong in a direction nobody notices. Missing values: fields left empty — no date, no address. An empty field is not a zero. Zero is a fact. Empty is an absence, and treating an absence as a zero corrupts every average it touches. Inconsistent entries: the same town written three ways, so a filter for one spelling silently misses the other two. And stale records: addresses of people who moved two years ago, customers marked active who asked to leave. Stale data is data that was true once. It is the hardest disease to see, because every field looks plausible.

The cure is not brilliance. The cure is a routine: decide the columns, decide the format for each column, enter data the same way every time, and spend a short regular session removing duplicates and filling or flagging gaps. I will not prescribe the length of the session, because your table is not mine. I will prescribe the regularity. Tables decay the way gardens do — gradually, then visibly. A small weeding, often, beats a heroic rescue, rarely. Also, keep a copy. Before any large cleanup or change, save a copy of the table as it was, with the date in its name. A copy is cheap. Regret is expensive, and undo buttons have limits that regret does not respect.

Here is the guided moment for this lesson. Picture a table you actually use — a contacts list, a budget, a list of anything. Name its rows out loud: one row is one what? Then name its columns: what kind of fact lives in each? Now find, in your mind, one violation: a row that is not the same kind of thing as the others, a column holding two kinds of facts, a duplicate you already suspect. One violation is enough. You have just audited a table, which is a professional act performed with no equipment. If you found no violation, either your table is unusually well kept or you should look again after this lesson ends. Both outcomes are informative.

Two tables deserve a word before we close, because our business lives in them. The first is the predictions record from lesson one, and now you can see its anatomy: each row is one prediction, made on one date. The columns are the date, what was predicted, what actually happened, and the verdict — hit or miss. Four columns, no decoration. Because every prediction is a row and the miss rows are never deleted, the hit rate is a simple count: hits divided by all rows, misses included. That is why the table's shape is its honesty. Delete the miss rows and the same arithmetic produces a perfect record and a worthless one. The second table is the advertising log: each row is one advertisement on one day, with columns for how many people saw it, how many clicked, and what it cost. Three honest columns there let the business compute, any evening, the cost per click: total cost divided by total clicks. If an advertisement cost fifty dollars and produced one hundred clicks, fifty divided by one hundred is zero point five — fifty cents per click. Whether fifty cents is good depends on what a click is worth, which is a business question, not an arithmetic one. Arithmetic answers how much. It does not answer whether you should. Remember which questions belong to which department.

A word on databases, briefly, so the term does not intimidate you later. A database is a system for holding many tables and enforcing their rules — formats, required fields, no duplicates of a chosen key — automatically, at a scale a spreadsheet cannot comfortably reach. When our business has eight hundred customers, a spreadsheet is sufficient and superior, because the owner can see everything. When it has eight hundred thousand, a database earns its keep. The concepts do not change: rows, columns, records, fields. Only the machinery grows. Anyone who tells you their database has transcended rows and columns is selling something. Rows and columns are not a limitation of small tools. They are the shape of organised fact.

Finally, a warning about the most dangerous spreadsheet feature: the silent edit. Anyone can change a number in a cell, and the table keeps no memory of the change. This is convenient and hazardous in equal measure. For any table that matters, keep the raw version untouched — the table as the data arrived — and do your sorting, filtering, and correcting in a working copy. Raw means unedited, exactly as collected. Working copy means the version you may improve. If your improvements turn out to be mistakes, the raw version lets you start again. Professionals separate these two without thinking. Amateurs merge them and then argue from memory about what the original said, which brings us back to lesson one: memory is a poor storage device. The raw table is the record. Guard it.

Let me slow down on one calculation, because it is the one our business will repeat weekly: the hit rate on the predictions record, done with the table open in front of us. Suppose the record holds sixty rows — sixty predictions, each with its verdict. Count the hit rows: thirty-nine. Count the miss rows: twenty-one. Check the addition before anything else: thirty-nine plus twenty-one is sixty, which matches the number of rows, so no verdict is missing and none is counted twice. That check takes five seconds and catches a category of error that embarrasses professionals. Now divide: thirty-nine divided by sixty is zero point six five. Times one hundred: sixty-five percent. The honest sentence is: sixty-five percent of sixty predictions were hits, twenty-one were misses, and here is the whole list. Every number in that sentence can be traced to rows. That traceability — from a headline figure down to the individual records under it — is what separates a table's answer from a person's impression. If a figure cannot be traced to rows, it did not come from the table. It came from someone, and someone is not a source.

The same discipline applies to money. The advertising log for one month holds thirty rows, one per day. Add the cost column: the month cost four hundred and fifty dollars. Add the clicks column: nine hundred clicks. Cost per click for the month is four hundred and fifty divided by nine hundred, which is zero point five — fifty cents, the same figure as before, now built from a whole month instead of a single day. Notice what the table gave us: not just the answer, but the audit trail. If the owner disputes fifty cents, you do not argue. You open the rows and add again, together. Tables end arguments that opinions prolong. This is not a small benefit in a business, or in a family, or anywhere else people share money.

Now consider what happens when two tables must agree. The customer table says eight hundred customers. The order table — one row per order — holds one thousand one hundred orders, each naming the customer who placed it. Ask the order table how many distinct customers appear in it, and suppose the answer is seven hundred and ninety. Ten customers in the customer table have never ordered, or their orders were recorded under a duplicate name, or the customer table carries ten ghosts. The disagreement is not a failure. The disagreement is information: it tells you exactly where to look. Two honest tables that disagree teach you more than one table that has never been checked against anything. Cross-checking — comparing what two records say about the same world — is the cheapest audit in existence, and the spreadsheet makes it a ten-minute job. Do it before you trust either table with a decision.

A practical word on naming and dates, because more tables die of sloppiness here than of any disease I listed. Name files so a stranger can find the right one: the table's subject, and the date it was saved, in the name itself. Inside the table, use one date style. I do not mind which style you choose. I mind deeply that you choose one. A column where January the fifth appears as five one, one five, and the fifth of January will sort wrongly, filter wrongly, and eventually be read wrongly by a tired person at a consequential moment. Consistency looks like pedantry from the outside. From the inside, it is load-bearing. The same applies to names of people and places: pick the spelling the person uses, use it every time, and let the spreadsheet's find function confirm there are no strays before you report any count that depends on it.

One more summary measure belongs in your kit, because tables invite it and novices misuse it: the range. The range is the largest value minus the smallest. Our Monday orders ran from ten dollars to one hundred dollars, so the range is ninety dollars. The range tells you the spread — how far apart the extremes sit. It is honest and fragile in equal measure: one unusual order moves it completely. Report it, by all means, but report it beside the median, which the unusual order cannot bully. A typical honest summary of a column is three numbers together: the median for the typical case, the mean for where the total sits, and the range for how wide the spread runs. Three numbers, each doing one job, none pretending to do the others. That is what a summary is supposed to be: smaller than the table, faithful to the table.

And a final caution, about empty rows and totals rows living inside the table itself. If your table contains a totals row — a row that is the sum of the other rows — then any count of rows counts the total as if it were a case, and any sum of the column adds the total to itself. I have seen a business report nine hundred customers from a table of eight hundred customers, one totals row, and ninety-nine duplicates it had not yet removed. The arithmetic was flawless. The table was lying about what its rows were. Keep totals outside the data, or clearly below a blank line, and count your rows before you compute anything. One row, one thing. The totals row is not a thing. It is arithmetic wearing a row's clothing.

You now hold the whole of lesson two, and it is deliberately unglamorous: rows, columns, records, fields, four diseases, a dated copy, a raw version kept safe. Unglamorous is not a criticism. Foundations are unglamorous. The glamorous failures I am called to examine, in business after business, stand on tables nobody weeded.

One more idea earns its place before the recap, because it decides whether a table grows gracefully or collapses: the key. A key is a field that identifies each row uniquely — a customer number, an order number, something that belongs to that row and no other. Names are poor keys. Two customers can share a name, and one customer can change theirs. A number assigned once, never reused, never edited, is a good key. With keys, two tables can be joined: the order table's customer number finds the customer's row in the customer table, and suddenly you can ask questions neither table answers alone — which town produces the largest orders, which month brought the customers who stayed longest. Joining is powerful and dangerous in the usual proportion: a join on a sloppy key manufactures confident nonsense at industrial speed. Check the key first. Then join. In that order, every time.

Also, briefly: a table should record when it was last updated, and by what rule new rows arrive. A customer table fed by the website behaves differently from one typed up after trade shows. The provenance of a table — where its rows came from — belongs written at the top of the file, in plain words, where a future reader cannot miss it. Provenance means the origin and history of a thing. Future readers include future you, who will have forgotten, as we established in lesson one. Write it for them. They are relying on you.

Let me work one filtering example completely, because filtering is where beginners first feel a table answer back. The owner asks: of the customers who joined this year, how many bought a second time? Start with the full table: eight hundred rows. Filter one: keep only rows whose first-purchase date falls in this year. Suppose three hundred rows remain. Those three hundred are now your whole — your denominator — for this question only. Filter two is not needed; instead, count within those rows the ones marked yes for a second purchase. Suppose the count is one hundred and five. Divide: one hundred and five divided by three hundred is zero point three five — thirty-five percent. Compare honestly with the whole-table figure from earlier: thirty percent of all eight hundred customers bought twice, but thirty-five percent of this year's three hundred did. Both are correct. They answer different questions because their denominators differ. Most arguments about percentages in business are, underneath, arguments about which denominator was quietly chosen. Bring the denominator into the open and half of those arguments end on the spot. I regard that as a public service.

And one sorting story, short, because it shows what sorting is for. Sort the predictions record by date and read down the verdict column. Early rows: miss, hit, miss, hit, hit. Later rows: hit, hit, miss, hit, hit, hit. Nothing in that glance proves the business improved — sixty rows is a modest count, and lesson three will teach you how modest — but the sorted table lets you see the sequence, and sequence is where improvement, if it exists, would live. Unsorted, the same facts are a soup. Sorted, they are a story you can interrogate. That is the entire case for the humble spreadsheet: it turns soup into sequence, piles into tables, and impressions into counts that can be traced back to rows. No magic. Just structure, kept.

A closing practical note on sharing tables, since our business will send its record to others and receive theirs. When you send a table, send the whole table, not the filtered view you happened to be admiring. A filtered view sent as if it were the whole is how honest people accidentally mislead: the recipient computes percentages against a denominator they cannot see is partial. If you must send a part, label it a part, in the file name and at the top of the sheet, with the size of the whole stated beside it. Thirty-nine hits out of sixty rows, twenty-one of them misses, travels honestly. Thirty-nine hits, alone, is a number on tour without its chaperone. We met that failure in lesson one as the missing denominator. In tables it has an address: it lives in the filtered view, exported carelessly. You know its address now. Do not forward its mail.

Recap, in order. One: a table is rows and columns — one row per case, one column per kind of fact, in one format. Two: a record is one complete row, and a field is one cell where a row and a column meet. Three: a spreadsheet holds the table and does the arithmetic — sorting to reveal, filtering to narrow, never to delete from your thinking. Four: a proportion is the part divided by the whole, and a percentage is that, times one hundred — thirty percent of our eight hundred customers bought twice, and the denominator travels with the figure. Five: the mean is the total divided by the count; the median is the middle value; when a few values are huge, ask for both. Six: tables suffer duplicates, missing values, inconsistent entries, and staleness; the cure is a routine, plus a dated copy before any large change. Seven: keep the raw table untouched and work in a copy.

One habit to take away, small enough to survive a busy week. Every time you open a table that matters, spend the first minute counting its rows and reading its column headings aloud, even silently. That minute tells you what the table claims to be. Every error in this lesson — the totals row counted as a customer, the filtered view mistaken for the whole, the duplicate inflating the count — announces itself in that first minute to a person who counts rows before computing anything. Professionals are not faster than you. They simply check the load-bearing things first, in a fixed order, every time. This lesson has given you the order. Use it in that order and the humble spreadsheet will repay you for years.

Next, the questions on this lesson, about what was taught here and nothing else. The full text stays open beside them. Going back to read is learning, not cheating. Keep the raw file, keep the dated copy, and keep the miss rows exactly where they belong: in the table, counted. A table kept this way will still contain errors — all real tables do — but they will be the findable kind, sitting in named columns, in consistent formats, where a careful person with a spreadsheet and a free hour can hunt them down one by one. That is all structure ever promises, and it is plenty. It will not make a dishonest person honest, and it will not rescue a question that was never worth asking, but it will make honesty easy and dishonesty visible, which in practice is most of what a working business, or a working science, ever gets from its tools.
In lesson three, we leave the tables we have and ask a harder question: how asking some people can teach you about all people — samples and populations. Bring your curiosity; the rest is provided.

lessons.title: Samples and populations: asking some to learn about all
paragraphs: Good to see you. Today AI and Computing earns its keep. I am Professor Juhani Korhonen, and this is lesson three of six in Data — Where It Lives and What It Proves: samples and populations — asking some to learn about all. Lessons one and two gave you records and tables: observations, kept whole, in rows and columns. Today we ask what happens when you cannot observe everyone, which is most of the time, and must learn about a whole group by examining a part of it. Done properly, this is one of the great intellectual tools of the modern world. Done carelessly, it produces confident nonsense with a spreadsheet attached. We will do it properly. I write the units on the board before opinions, every time. Bring your curiosity, and bring one poll or survey you have seen this month — we will need examples of togetherness mistaken for cause, and the supply, regrettably, is not limited; the rest is provided.

Definitions first, as always. A population is the whole group you want to learn about — all of them, every one. The word does not require people. A population can be all the customers of a business, all the orders shipped last year, all the voters in a town, or all the predictions in a record. A sample is the part of the population you actually examine. A census is the special case where the sample is the population: you examined everyone. A census is exact and usually impractical. Our marketing business has eight hundred customers. It could, in principle, ask all eight hundred whether they are satisfied. That would be a census. In practice it will ask some of them, and the asking itself takes time, and some will not answer, and so it will work from a sample, as will you, in nearly every real situation you ever face.

The central question of this lesson is one sentence: how can some stand for all? The answer is also one sentence, and then we will spend the lesson earning it. A sample can stand for a population when every member of the population had a fair chance of being chosen, and the choosing was not rigged by convenience, enthusiasm, or hope. A sample chosen that way is called a random sample. Random does not mean haphazard. Random means chosen by a method that gives every member a known, equal chance and gives the chooser no say in who lands in the sample. Drawing names from a well-mixed hat is random. Asking the first fifty customers who walk in on a Saturday is not random, however innocent it feels. Saturday morning customers are not all customers. They are the customers who shop on Saturday mornings, and they differ from the others in ways you cannot see from inside the sample.

Let me make the stakes concrete with our business. The owner wants to know what share of all eight hundred customers would recommend the business to a friend. He emails a short survey to a random sample of two hundred customers — chosen by the spreadsheet, every customer equally likely, no names picked by hand. One hundred and sixty reply. Of those, one hundred and twelve say yes, they would recommend it. Divide: one hundred and twelve divided by one hundred and sixty is zero point seven. Seventy percent of the respondents said yes. Now the exact sentence the owner may say: about seventy percent of our customers would probably recommend us. Note the words about and probably, which are not weakness. They are accuracy. The sample said seventy percent. The population — all eight hundred — will not be exactly seventy percent. It might be sixty-seven. It might be seventy-three. The sample gives you an estimate, which is a number offered as close to the truth, with the honest understanding that it is not the truth itself. An estimate is not a failed measurement. It is a successful one, correctly labelled.

How close is close? That depends mainly on the size of the sample, and here is the fact that surprises everyone the first time: it depends on the size of the sample, not on the size of the population. A random sample of one hundred and sixty from eight hundred customers tells you roughly as much as a random sample of one hundred and sixty from eight hundred thousand customers. The population can grow a thousandfold and the sample's precision barely moves, provided the sample was truly random. What moves precision is the sample's own size. Small samples wobble. Large samples settle. You met the small version in lesson one: six clicks versus three clicks, out of one hundred, was noise. Here is the settled version: with a random sample of one thousand people, a result of seventy percent will usually sit within about three percentage points of the population's true value — somewhere between sixty-seven and seventy-three. That wobble has a name: the margin of error. The margin of error is the amount by which a sample result may reasonably differ from the population value, purely because you asked some instead of all. When a poll reports seventy percent with a margin of error of three points, it is saying: our best estimate is seventy, and the honest range around it runs from sixty-seven to seventy-three. A poll that reports the percentage without the margin is withholding half the finding. Ask for both, every time, the way you ask for the denominator.

Do not memorise the numbers three and one thousand as magic. Understand the shape. Quadruple the sample and you roughly halve the margin of error. A sample of one hundred carries a margin near ten points — too wide for fine decisions, fine for coarse ones. A sample of four hundred carries a margin near five points. A sample of one thousand carries a margin near three. Precision is bought with sample size, and the price rises steeply: each halving of the margin costs four times the asking. Our business, with its survey of one hundred and sixty replies, lives with a margin near eight points. Seventy percent, honestly reported, means the truth is probably somewhere between about sixty-two and seventy-eight. That is still useful. It rules out disaster and it rules out perfection, which is more knowledge than the owner had on Monday. Data rarely gives certainty. It gives narrower ignorance, and narrower ignorance, compounded over many decisions, is what competence is made of.

Now the failures, because samples fail in patterned ways and the patterns have names. The first failure is a biased sample. A sample is biased when the method of choosing systematically favours some members of the population over others, so the sample differs from the population in a direction, not merely by chance. Surveying customers through the business's social media page samples the customers who follow the page — younger, more enthusiastic, more online — and their answers will flatter the business in a consistent direction. Bias is worse than noise. Noise wobbles around the truth and shrinks as the sample grows. Bias points away from the truth and does not shrink at all: a biased sample of ten thousand is precisely, confidently wrong. Size cannot cure bias. Only the choosing method can. This is why I am unimpressed by very large samples gathered carelessly. A large biased sample is a large error with good posture.

The second failure is non-response. Non-response means the people chosen for the sample who did not answer. In our survey, two hundred were asked and one hundred and sixty replied, so forty did not. The response rate is the share who did answer: one hundred and sixty divided by two hundred is zero point eight — eighty percent. That is a good rate. Trouble begins at low rates, because non-respondents are rarely a random slice of the chosen. People with strong feelings answer surveys. People who are furious answer. People who are delighted answer. The vast, mildly content middle often does not, and so a survey with a twenty percent response rate may describe the extremes of your customers while claiming to describe your customers. When someone shows you survey results, the second question — after how was the sample chosen — is: what share of those chosen actually answered? A finding built on a small, self-selected fraction of a sample is an anecdote collection wearing a percentage, and lesson one already taught you what to call that.

The third failure is the leading question, which corrupts the sample's answers rather than its membership. A question that pushes — would you agree our friendly service deserves five stars — does not measure opinion. It manufactures it. The respondents are real, the sample may be random, and the data are still worthless, because the instrument bent every reading in one direction, like the uncalibrated scale from lesson one. Honest questions are flat: how would you rate the service, from one to five. Flat questions feel less exciting. They have the compensating virtue of measuring something.

Here is the guided moment for this lesson. Think of a claim you have heard that begins with words like most people, customers prefer, or voters want. Someone, somewhere, asked some and announced all. Reconstruct the asking. Who exactly was asked — can you picture them? How were they chosen — by a method that gave everyone a fair chance, or by whoever happened to be nearby, online, or willing? How many answered, out of how many asked? And what range would the margin of error honestly allow around the headline number? Run those four checks silently on the next such claim you meet in the wild. You will find that most claims of this kind cannot survive the second check. That is not cynicism. That is sampling theory, applied at walking pace.

Our predictions record offers a different, quieter application. Sixty predictions, thirty-nine hits, twenty-one misses — a sixty-five percent hit rate, computed in lesson two. Now ask the sampling question: what population does that record describe? It describes those sixty predictions exactly — for them, it is a census, not a sample, and sixty-five percent is not an estimate but a count. The moment someone says the record proves the business will hit sixty-five percent of future predictions, the sixty rows have been silently promoted into a sample of the future, and the future is a population with opinions of its own: different conditions, different difficulty, different luck. The honest claim is narrower and stronger: of the sixty predictions made and kept whole, thirty-nine were hits. What the future holds, the record informs but does not settle. Confusing a census of the past with a guarantee about the future is the most respectable error in this entire class, and it is still an error.

One more distinction, because it governs real money. Sometimes you do not need a sample at all. If the population is small and the records already exist — all orders last month, all complaints this year — use the records. That is a census of stored data, and it beats any survey. Sampling is for when observing everyone is impossible, expensive, or destructive. You cannot taste every bottle to check the batch. You can count every complaint in the file. Choose the census when the file exists. Choose the sample when it does not. And when you choose the sample, spend your effort on the choosing — random, fair, documented — because no arithmetic performed afterwards can repair a choosing that was rigged at the start. Arithmetic is powerful. It is not resurrection.

Let me also give you the phrase that protects you in meetings: representative. A representative sample is one that resembles the population in the respects that matter for the question — similar mix of new and old customers, of big and small orders, of every group the conclusion will be applied to. Random choosing is how you earn representativeness without hand-arranging it. The moment someone hand-arranges a sample to look representative — picking, by eye, a nice mix — they have reintroduced their own judgement into the choosing, and their judgement, however experienced, is a bias with a biography. Trust the hat. Trust the spreadsheet's random draw. Do not trust the hand, including your own. Especially your own, because yours is the hand whose biases you cannot see.

A worked example from election polling will fix the margin of error in your mind better than any definition. A town has fifty thousand voters. A polling firm draws a random sample of one thousand of them and finds that five hundred and twenty intend to vote for one candidate. Five hundred and twenty divided by one thousand is zero point five two — fifty-two percent. The firm reports fifty-two percent, margin of error three points. The honest reading: the candidate's true support in the town is probably between forty-nine and fifty-five percent. Note what follows and what does not. It does not follow that the candidate leads, because the opponent's forty-eight percent carries the same margin, and the two ranges overlap. It does not follow that the candidate will win, because intentions are not votes and three weeks remain. What follows is narrower ignorance, exactly as promised: support is somewhere near half, the race is close, and anyone announcing a certain outcome from this poll is selling certainty the sample never contained. When the sample grows to four thousand, the margin shrinks to about one and a half points, and the same fifty-two percent becomes a genuinely informative lead. Same town. Same percentage. Different sample size, different knowledge. The percentage is the headline. The sample size is the news.

Now, a technique our business can actually afford: stratification. Stratified sampling means dividing the population into groups — strata — and sampling from each group deliberately, so no group is missed by chance. The business's customers divide naturally into new customers, under a year, and established customers, a year or more. A pure random sample of two hundred from eight hundred might, by luck, draw only thirty new customers, too few to say anything about them separately. A stratified sample draws, say, one hundred new and one hundred established, on purpose, and can then speak about each group as well as about the whole, combining the groups in their true proportions when it reports the total. Stratification is not the hand-picking I warned against. The groups are defined in advance, every member still has a fair chance within their group, and the proportions are corrected in the arithmetic, openly. The difference between stratification and rigging is the same as the difference between a recipe and a guess: written down in advance, applied the same way every time, and available for inspection.

Let me also name the sample you should never trust, however large it grows: the convenience sample. A convenience sample is whoever was easiest to reach — the customers who happened to visit this week, the followers who happened to see the post, the friends who happened to answer the message. Convenience samples are not worthless for every purpose. They are excellent for discovering that a problem exists: if twelve of this week's visitors independently mention the same broken page, the page is broken, and you need no random sample to justify fixing it. They are worthless for measuring how common anything is, because ease of reaching is itself a filter, and the filter's shape is unknown. Existence, yes. Prevalence, no. Prevalence means how widespread a thing is in the population. Keep those two jobs separate and convenience samples will serve you honestly in the first and never betray you in the second.

There is one more quiet assumption to drag into the light: the population must be defined before the sample means anything. All our customers sounds precise until you ask whether it includes the customer who bought once, nine years ago, and moved abroad. Or the forty ghosts from lesson two — the duplicates still sitting in the table. A sample drawn from a dirty table inherits the dirt. Seven hundred and sixty real people and forty duplicate rows will be sampled as if they were eight hundred people, and the duplicated customers will be asked twice as often as they should be, in proportion to their ghostliness. This is why lesson two came before lesson three. Clean tables first. Fair samples second. Conclusions third, in that order, and any consultant who proposes reversing the order should be charged by the hour for the entertainment.

A word about very small populations, because small businesses live there. If the population is forty — forty major clients, say — a sample of twenty is not a shortcut. It is half a census performed to avoid the other half, and the margin of error on twenty is wide enough to embarrass the saving. With small populations, either examine everyone or state plainly that you examined a part and the part may mislead. There is no third option, and sampling theory, which is generous to large populations, offers small ones no discount. The honest small-business move is usually the census: forty clients can be telephoned. Eight hundred customers cannot, not by Friday. Let the size of the population choose the method, and let the method be written down before the first call is made.

Finally, the sentence I most want installed. Whenever a number about all is built from some, the finding is not the number. The finding is the number, plus the size of the sample, plus how the sample was chosen, plus the share who answered. Four parts. A report missing any of the four is a story with pages torn out, and you now know enough to notice the tearing. Demand the missing pages politely, in writing, before money moves. If they cannot be produced, you have learned something about the report that the report was designed to prevent you learning. Price it accordingly.

One more worked check, on the advertising numbers, because sampling hides there too. The business shows its advertisement to a sample of the town — say the platform delivers it to two thousand people chosen by the platform's own machinery — and one hundred and forty click. One hundred and forty divided by two thousand is zero point zero seven: a seven percent click rate. The owner wants to say seven percent of the town would click. Stop him, kindly. The two thousand were not a random sample of the town. The platform chose them by its own rules, which favour people likely to click, because platforms are paid when people click. The seven percent is a true fact about those two thousand deliveries. As an estimate of the town, it is biased upward by an amount nobody can compute, because the choosing method is a trade secret. This is the modern shape of sampling failure: the sample is enormous, the arithmetic is perfect, and the choosing belongs to someone whose interests differ from yours. Size cannot cure bias. I said it earlier and I repeat it here, because this is the form in which you will meet it monthly for the rest of your working life.

And a brief honourable mention for the pilot. A pilot study is a small sample used to test the method itself — does the survey question confuse people, does the form work, how long does an interview take — before the real sample is drawn. Pilots are not findings. A pilot of twenty customers that returns fourteen yes answers has taught you that the question can be asked, not that seventy percent of customers agree. Confusing a pilot with a finding is a category error I have watched grown companies commit in print. Run pilots. Learn from them. Publish nothing from them except what the method taught you.

A short historical note, because it shows the price of ignoring all of this at national scale. In nineteen thirty-six, a famous magazine polled over two million people and predicted a landslide winner in an American presidential election. The sample was gigantic. It was also drawn from car registrations and telephone directories, in a depression, when cars and telephones belonged disproportionately to the wealthier half of the country. The poorer half voted the other way, and the magazine's prediction failed completely, while a rival using a far smaller, properly drawn sample called the result correctly. Two million biased answers lost to a few thousand fair ones. I tell this story in every sampling class I teach, because students remember stories longer than rules, and this story is the rule: the choosing is the science. The counting is arithmetic. Anyone can count. Choosing fairly is the discipline, and it is decided before a single answer arrives, by a person, in advance, in writing — or it is decided afterwards, by the bias, without asking anyone's permission.

One distinction remains, small in wording and large in consequence: sampling error versus every other kind of error. Sampling error is the wobble that remains even when everything is done right — the gap between a fair sample and its population, caused by chance alone. The margin of error measures that wobble and nothing else. It does not cover a leading question, a biased draw, a dirty table, or a low response rate. Those are separate failures, unmeasured by the margin, and usually larger. This is why a reported margin of error can coexist with a badly wrong result: the margin honestly describes the one error that was controlled, while the uncontrolled errors stand offstage, unpriced. When you read a poll, read the margin as a floor under the uncertainty, never as the whole of it. The whole of it is the margin plus everything the method got wrong, and the method section — how they chose, how many answered — is where those errors are confessed, for readers patient enough to look. Be that reader. It takes four minutes, and it is the difference between consuming a finding and auditing one.

Recap, in order. One: the population is the whole group you want to learn about; the sample is the part you actually examine; a census examines everyone. Two: a sample stands for a population when the choosing is random — every member with a fair chance, and no hand on the scale. Three: a sample gives an estimate, not the exact population value, and the margin of error states honestly how far off it may be. Four: precision grows with sample size, not population size, and each halving of the margin costs roughly four times the sample. Five: bias is a choosing method that points away from the truth, and no sample size cures it. Six: watch the response rate — those who did not answer are data too, by their absence. Seven: a record of the past is a census of that past; treating it as a guarantee about the future is an error, however respectable.

Before the questions, fix the four checks in order, because order is a memory aid and this set deserves one. First: who was asked, exactly — can you picture the actual people, or only a fog with a percentage in it? Second: how were they chosen — by a method that gave every member of the population a fair chance, or by convenience, enthusiasm, or an algorithm with its own interests? Third: how many answered, out of how many asked — and is the gap between those numbers small enough to ignore, which it rarely is? Fourth: what range does the margin of error honestly allow — and does the headline conclusion still stand at the far edge of that range, or does it quietly fall over? A claim that survives all four checks has earned provisional belief, which is the strongest currency this class deals in. A claim that fails the second check has failed entirely, whatever its sample size, because bias does not shrink. Hold that hierarchy — choosing first, size second — and you will read every survey, poll, and platform report for the rest of your life with better eyes than the people who published them expected you to have. That is the lesson. The questions merely check whether it landed.

Next, the questions on this lesson. The full text stays open beside them, and going back to read is learning, not cheating. Carry the four parts in your pocket the way you carry the three questions from lesson one, because the two sets work together: the three questions test whether data exists at all, and the four parts test whether a sample's number deserves to travel from some to all. Most published findings fail one set or the other within a minute of honest inspection, and the minute is never wasted, because what survives it can be built on.

One sentence to take with you, and then we are done. Ask some, by a fair method, in sufficient number, and report the range as faithfully as the result — and some will teach you about all, within stated limits, which is all that honest knowledge ever claims.

In lesson four we take up the most abused pair of words in all of data: correlation and causation, and the gap between them, which is wide enough to lose a business in. Bring your curiosity; the rest is provided.
