lessons.title: Correlation, causation, and the gap between them
paragraphs: Good to see you. Today AI and Computing earns its keep. I am Professor Juhani Korhonen, and this is lesson four of six in Data — Where It Lives and What It Proves: correlation, causation, and the gap between them. This is the lesson where data most often gets promoted beyond its rank. Two things move together, and within a sentence one of them is causing the other, and within a paragraph money is being spent on the strength of it. We will slow that promotion down until it has to show its papers. I write the units on the board before opinions, every time. Bring your curiosity, and bring your suspicion of any sentence in which one thing is said to drive, boost, or deliver another on the evidence of a single chart; the rest is provided.

Definitions, exactly, because this lesson lives or dies on them. Two things are correlated when they tend to move together: when one is high, the other tends to be high — or, in the other direction, when one is high, the other tends to be low. Correlation is a pattern in recorded observations. Nothing more. Causation is a different claim entirely: causation means one thing makes the other happen — change the first and, because of that change, the second changes. Correlation is observed. Causation is inferred, argued, and, if you are fortunate and careful, tested. The gap between them is the subject of this lesson, and the gap is wide. The sentence to carry out of this room is the oldest in statistics, and it has not expired: correlation is not causation. Two things moving together is a clue. A clue is the beginning of an investigation. It is not the end of one.

Our marketing business supplies the first example. Over one year, the months with the highest advertising spend are also the months with the highest revenue. Spend and revenue rise together and fall together. The correlation is real — it sits in the advertising log and the accounts, in rows, checkable. The owner concludes: advertising causes revenue, so double the advertising. Perhaps. But look at the calendar. The highest-revenue months are November and December, when customers buy for the holidays regardless of what any business does. The business also advertises most in November and December, because that is when the customers are buying. A third thing — the season — is pushing both. This pattern has a name: a confounder. A confounder is a third factor that influences both things you are comparing, making them move together without either one causing the other. The season does not merely muddy this example. It may explain all of it. Advertising might add a great deal, a little, or nothing, and the correlation, by itself, cannot tell you which. Anyone who reads a correlation as a cause without hunting for confounders is not analysing. They are applauding.

Let me give you the classic absurd case, because absurdity is a teaching instrument. In many towns, ice cream sales and drowning deaths are strongly correlated across the year: both peak in the same months. Ice cream does not cause drowning, and banning ice cream would save no swimmers. The confounder is summer heat: heat sells ice cream, and heat sends people swimming, and swimming, occasionally and tragically, involves drowning. Two effects of one cause, marching together, impersonating a cause and its effect. Whenever you meet a correlation, your first professional act is to ask: what third thing could be pushing both? Do not ask whether there is a confounder, as if it were a remote possibility. Ask which confounder it is, as if it were certainly present and merely unnamed. That posture — assume a confounder until the hunt comes back empty — will protect you more reliably than any formula in this class.

The second impostor is reversed direction. Correlation is symmetric: if A moves with B, then B moves with A, and the pattern alone cannot tell you which, if either, is the cause. Our business finds that its most loyal customers are the ones who receive its email newsletter. Does the newsletter create loyalty? Or do loyal customers — people already fond of the business — sign up for newsletters at higher rates? Both stories fit the same correlation perfectly. The arrow of causation points one way in the first story and the opposite way in the second, and the data, as collected, are silent about arrows. Businesses spend heavily on the wrong arrow every year: they observe what their best customers do and then push all customers to do it, as if the behaviour manufactured the loyalty rather than merely advertising it. Sometimes it does. Often it is the loyalty wearing a uniform. The correlation cannot tell you which uniform it is.

The third impostor is coincidence, and it deserves respect because with enough data lying around, coincidence is guaranteed to produce beautiful correlations. If you track a hundred pairs of unrelated things, some pairs will march together for a while by pure chance — lesson one's noise, wearing a correlation's clothing. The more pairs you examine, the more striking coincidences you will find, and the finding will feel like discovery precisely because you examined so many. This is why a correlation discovered by trawling — by testing everything against everything until something lines up — deserves deep suspicion, while the same correlation, predicted in advance for a stated reason, deserves a hearing. A prediction made in advance, recorded, and then checked: you have met that discipline before. It is the predictions record again. The record's whole design — write it before, keep it whole — is a machine for separating real patterns from trawled coincidences, in business exactly as in science.

Now, the honest question: if correlation cannot prove causation, what can? The strongest everyday tool is the experiment. An experiment means you deliberately change one thing, hold everything else as steady as you can, and compare the outcome against a group where you changed nothing. That unchanged group is the control group. The group you changed is the treatment group. Our business can run one this month. It wants to know whether its new advertisement actually causes more enquiries, or whether enquiries would have risen anyway. It shows the new advertisement to a randomly chosen half of its audience and the old advertisement to the other half, in the same week, at the same spend per person. Randomly chosen — lesson three's machinery, doing its job — so the two groups are alike in every way except the advertisement. Suppose the new advertisement's group produces one hundred and twenty enquiries from ten thousand viewers, and the old advertisement's group produces one hundred enquiries from ten thousand viewers. One hundred and twenty against one hundred, on equal denominators, in the same week. Now the causal claim has earned a hearing: the only systematic difference between the groups is the advertisement, so the difference in enquiries is credited to it — provisionally, with the counts stated, and with lesson three's warning attached that even twenty extra enquiries on these numbers could partly be luck. Repeat the experiment and the credit firms up. That is how causation is actually established in practice: not by one dramatic proof, but by controlled comparisons, repeated, with confounders designed out in advance rather than argued away afterwards.

Notice what the experiment did that observation could not. In observation, the season, the audience, and the advertisement all change together, tangled. In the experiment, the design untangles them before the data arrive: same week kills the season as a confounder, random assignment kills the audience difference, equal spend kills the budget difference. Design beats argument. An hour of design before the fact is worth a month of arguing after it, and considerably cheaper in temper.

Where experiments are impossible — you cannot randomly assign people a childhood, a town, or a decade — causation must be argued from converging evidence: the correlation is strong, it appears in many settings, the supposed cause comes before the effect in time, and a plausible mechanism connects them. A mechanism is an account of how the cause would produce the effect, step by step. Timing matters absolutely: a cause must precede its effect. If revenue rose in March and the campaign began in April, the campaign did not cause the March rise, whatever the annual correlation says, and you would be surprised how often that elementary check is skipped in reports written by people with salaries. Hold the checklist: strength, consistency across settings, timing, mechanism — and even with all four, the honest word is supports, not proves. In this class, proves is a word we spend rarely, and only where the design has earned it.

Here is the guided moment. Recall a causal claim you have heard recently — an advertisement causes sales, a policy causes crime to fall, a food causes energy. Do not attack it. Interrogate it, in order. First: what is the correlation actually observed, stripped of causal words? Say it in moving-together language only. Second: name one confounder — one third thing that could push both. If you cannot name one, you have not looked; look again, the season and wealth and age are confounders in a remarkable share of all claims. Third: could the arrow run backwards? Fourth: was there an experiment, or a comparison that resembles one? You have now done, in two minutes, the analysis that most published causal claims never receive. The claim may survive. Many do. It will at least have been examined by someone, which distinguishes your reading of it from nearly everyone's.

Apply the whole apparatus to the predictions record, because it is this class's standing example of honesty and I want its limits stated by me, not discovered by you. The record shows sixty predictions, thirty-nine hits, twenty-one misses, kept whole. Does that prove the business's method causes good predictions? Carefully. It proves the predictions were made in advance and that thirty-nine of sixty matched what happened. That is a fact about the record. The causal claim — the method, rather than luck, produced the hits — needs more: it needs the difficulty of the predictions stated, because predicting sunrise sixty times would also yield a fine record, and it needs a comparison — what would chance alone, or a simpler method, have scored on the same sixty questions? Without that comparison, the record is honest description, not causal proof. Honest description is valuable. It is the floor everything else stands on. But this class does not promote description into proof, for our own record any more than for a consultant's brochure. The standard is the standard, and it applies at home first.

One more term, because you will meet it in print: a spurious correlation is a correlation that is real in the numbers but meaningless in the world — produced by a confounder, by coincidence, or by both marching together. Spurious does not mean the arithmetic was wrong. The arithmetic is usually impeccable. It means the story pasted onto the arithmetic is false. Data do not lie, people say. Data do not speak, either. People speak for data, and the speaking is where the lying, and the erring, and occasionally the science, happens. Your job, trained by this class, is to audit the speaking.

Let me work the season example with actual numbers, so the confounder stops being an abstraction. Suppose the business spends four hundred dollars on advertising in June and earns four thousand dollars in revenue. In December it spends one thousand two hundred dollars and earns twelve thousand dollars. Spend tripled; revenue tripled; the correlation across the year looks immaculate. Now the confounder's arithmetic. December brings, let us say, three times the customer traffic of June, holidays being what they are. Revenue per advertising dollar is ten dollars in both months: four thousand over four hundred, twelve thousand over one thousand two hundred. The advertising did not become more effective in December. There were simply more buyers in the room, and both the spending and the earning were responses to their presence. The correlation between spend and revenue is real, and the causal story — spending drove the revenue — may still contain some truth, but the clean tripling belongs to the season. A business that doubles its June advertising on the strength of December's correlation will discover that June has no holidays hidden in it. I have watched this exact expenditure happen. The report afterwards blamed the advertisement. The advertisement was innocent. The calendar did it.

A second worked example, from the customer table this time. The business notices that customers who buy on Mondays spend more per order than customers who buy on Fridays. The correlation is in the table; sort it and see. A causal story arrives instantly: Monday shoppers are serious shoppers, so aim the best offers at Monday. But hunt the confounder first. Suppose businesses — offices, workshops, other firms — order on Mondays, at the week's start, in bulk, while individuals order on Fridays, in small quantities, for the weekend. Then the confounder is customer type: firms spend more and shop on Mondays; individuals spend less and shop on Fridays. The day is not causing the spending. The customer is causing both the day and the spending. Aim the best offers at firms, on whatever day they shop, and the business profits. Aim them at Monday, indiscriminately, and it discounts large Friday individuals and small Monday firms alike, having mistaken a calendar for a cause. Same table, same correlation, two strategies, only one of them aimed at the actual mechanism.

Now let me teach you the phrase that does the most work in this whole lesson, because you can use it in any meeting without giving offence: what else changed? When a result is credited to one cause — the new advertisement, the new price, the new manager — ask what else changed in the same period. Something always else changed. Seasons turn, competitors move, prices of supplies rise, a road closes, a holiday lands on a different weekday. The question does not deny the credited cause. It audits the credit. If the answer is a thoughtful list with reasons each item cannot explain the result, the causal claim grows stronger in front of you. If the answer is a blank look, you have learned that the claim was never examined, only asserted. Assertions are free. Examinations are the product. Buy examinations.

There is a special case worth isolating: the before-and-after comparison, which is the experiment's poor relation and the most common causal argument in business. Sales were X before the change and Y after it; therefore the change worked. The flaw is structural: before and after differ in time, and time brings everything else with it — season, trend, weather, news. A rising business makes many changes, and each change claims the rise that the trend was delivering anyway. The repair, when a true experiment is impossible, is a comparison group that lived through the same period without the change: another town, another product line, the customers who were not sent the offer. If the changed group rose ten percent and the unchanged group rose nine percent in the same weeks, the change's honest credit is about one point, not ten. That subtraction — the comparison group's change removed from the treatment group's change — is the single most valuable arithmetic habit in causal reasoning. It converts applause into estimate. Use it wherever two groups and two periods exist, which is more often than businesses realise.

A word, too, on dose. If a cause is real, more of it usually produces more of the effect, up to some limit: a dose-response pattern. Advertising that genuinely causes enquiries should, within reason, produce more enquiries at higher spend — not perfectly, not forever, but visibly. When doubling the spend produces nothing at all, repeatedly, the causal story weakens, however fine the original correlation looked. Dose is not proof either — a confounder can also rise with the dose, as December's traffic rises with December's spend — but a complete absence of dose-response is evidence against a cause, and evidence against deserves the same attention as evidence for. Symmetric standards, again: we grade our own favourite claims with the same instruments we aim at other people's. That symmetry is not politeness. It is what makes the instruments trustworthy when they finally say yes.

Let me close the teaching with the hierarchy, stated plainly, so you can rank any claim you meet. At the bottom: a single anecdote with a causal story — lesson one's weakest material, promoted without authority. Above it: a correlation, honestly measured, cause unknown. Above that: a correlation with confounders hunted, timing right, mechanism plausible, found in several settings. Above that: a before-and-after with a comparison group, differenced honestly. At the top, for everyday purposes: a controlled experiment, randomly assigned, repeated. Claims should be priced by their floor in this building. The tragedy of business data is not that low-floor claims exist — they are where inquiry starts — but that they are so often priced as penthouses. Your training is simply this: read the floor before admiring the view.

One more caution, on language, because language is where causal claims smuggle themselves past guards. Watch for verbs. Linked to, associated with, and rises with are correlation words — honest ones. Drives, boosts, delivers, and fuels are causation words. Reports frequently begin with the honest words in the headline's small print and graduate to the causal verbs by the second paragraph, without any new evidence arriving in between. The evidence did not change. Only the verbs did. Train your ear for the graduation. When you hear a causal verb, ask which floor of the hierarchy the speaker is standing on, and whether the rent for the higher floor was ever paid. You will find, often, that the entire causal claim is a verb choice. Verbs are cheap. Experiments are not. Prefer the people who pay.

And the mirror-image error, briefly, so you do not overcorrect: refusing all causal claims because none is perfect. That posture feels rigorous and is merely lazy. The experiment with random assignment, equal denominators, and repeated results is strong knowledge — strong enough to spend money on, carefully, in stages, watching the next results as they arrive. Science is not the refusal to conclude. It is concluding at exactly the strength the design has earned, and no stronger. A claim priced correctly can be acted on. A claim refused entirely cannot, and the business that refuses all claims will be out-competed by the business that prices them. Exactness, not timidity, is the virtue this class is building.

A brief note on a phrase you will now start hearing everywhere, precisely because you have a name for the thing it hides: studies show. Studies show a correlation, usually, in a particular population, under particular conditions, with confounders hunted to a particular depth. The phrase studies show compresses all of that into two words of borrowed authority. Decompress it, every time, with the instruments of this lesson: what moved with what, in whom, what else changed, which way might the arrow run, and was anything compared against a control? A study that survives decompression is worth your attention. A claim that cannot survive being stated precisely was never a finding. It was a fog with a citation. You are no longer required to breathe fog, in this class or out of it.

One more pattern completes the set, and it is the subtlest: the correlation that is real, causal, and still misread, because the cause works through a chain. Advertising may cause enquiries, enquiries may cause calls, and calls may cause sales. If the business measures only advertising against sales, the correlation will look weak and erratic, because two leaky links sit between them — many enquiries never call, many calls never buy. The weak correlation does not acquit the advertisement, and a strong one would not convict it either; the chain must be measured link by link, which the tables from lesson two make possible: advertisement rows against enquiry counts, enquiry rows against calls, calls against orders. Causal chains are where small businesses quietly misjudge their marketing for years, crediting the last link — the salesperson, the web page — for the whole chain's work, or blaming the first link for a break that happened at the third. Measure each link. Credit each link. Repair the broken link, which is usually not the one the argument is about.

Recap, in order. One: correlation means two things tend to move together; causation means one makes the other happen; the first is observed, the second must be earned. Two: a confounder is a third factor pushing both, and your first act on meeting any correlation is to hunt for it. Three: correlation cannot tell you the direction of the arrow — the cause may run backwards from the story being told. Four: trawling many pairs manufactures coincidences, while predictions recorded in advance earn a hearing. Five: an experiment — a treatment group, a control group, random assignment, everything else held steady — is the strongest everyday road to a causal claim. Six: where experiments are impossible, argue from strength, consistency, timing, and mechanism, and let the word be supports, not proves. Seven: even an honest record describes before it proves; the standard applies at home first.

One last exercise in imagination before the questions, because the next claim you meet will not wait for a convenient moment. Picture the owner, in January, holding a chart of last year's spend and revenue marching upward together, proposing to triple the advertising budget. You are the person in the room who has taken this lesson. You do not say correlation is not causation and sit down, although the sentence is true; slogans persuade nobody who holds a chart. You ask, in order: what else changed across those months — and let the season be named by the room, not by you. You ask what revenue per advertising dollar did in June versus December, and let the arithmetic — ten dollars in both — do the arguing. You ask whether a comparison exists: a product line that was not advertised, a town where the campaign did not run. And you propose the experiment: one month, two halves of the audience, randomly assigned, equal spend, enquiries counted. Notice the shape of what you have done. You have not blocked the owner. You have converted an act of faith into a testable question with a price tag of one month, which is what this entire class means by thinking with data. If the advertisement truly causes enquiries, the experiment will say so, and the budget can triple with evidence under it. If it does not, the business has purchased the truth at a discount. Either way the room wins, and either way you were the reason. That is the professional this course is building, one lesson at a time.

Answer them at the strength the lesson earned and no stronger: that instruction is a joke about causation, and also, not entirely, a joke. The serious version is the whole course in one line: conclude at the strength your evidence has earned, state the strength when you conclude, and let the record — kept whole, counted honestly, compared fairly — carry exactly the weight it can bear and not one gram more. That discipline, practised daily, is indistinguishable from wisdom at a distance.

Next, the questions on this lesson, with the full text open beside them — going back to read is learning, not cheating. Keep the question what else changed within reach at all times. It costs nothing, offends no one who is honest, and has ended more bad expenditures than any software I own. Questions of that quality are rare. You now own two sets of them — the three from lesson one, the four checks from lesson three, and this single sentence from lesson four — and together they will examine nearly any claim that data is asked to carry.

You came in, most likely, using the words correlation and causation almost interchangeably, as the world does. You leave with them separated by a gap you can measure: on one side, patterns observed in records; on the other, claims that must be earned by design, comparison, timing, and mechanism. That separation, maintained under pressure — under the pressure of a confident owner, a persuasive consultant, a beautiful chart, and your own hope that the expensive thing worked — is most of what separates a person who uses data from a person who is used by it. Hold the separation. It is the lesson. And when you catch yourself graduating a correlation into a cause in your own speech — you will; everyone does; the verbs are lying there polished and ready — correct yourself out loud, in the room, by name. Nothing builds a reputation for exactness faster than a person visibly refusing their own exaggeration, and nothing in this class is worth more than that reputation, because it is the asset every later claim you make will be priced against.
In lesson five, we turn to charts: the pictures drawn from data, which can tell the truth plainly or lean while appearing to merely stand there. Bring your curiosity; the rest is provided.

lessons.title: Charts that tell the truth and charts that lean
paragraphs: Good to see you. Today AI and Computing earns its keep. I am Professor Juhani Korhonen, and this is lesson five of six in Data — Where It Lives and What It Proves: charts that tell the truth and charts that lean. Every lesson so far has dealt with numbers in rows. Today the numbers put on pictures, because most people meet data as pictures — in reports, in presentations, in news, in the pitch deck of a person who would like some of your money. A chart is an argument made with geometry. It can be an honest argument or a leaning one, and the leaning is usually accomplished without changing a single number. I write the units on the board before opinions, every time. Bring your curiosity, and one chart from your own life that you are prepared to discover has been leaning at you for years; the rest, as ever, is provided, and the record of this class — all six lessons of it — stays open beside you.

First, what a chart is for. A chart translates numbers into shapes and lengths and positions, because the human eye compares lengths and positions faster and more reliably than it compares digits in a table. A good chart makes a true pattern visible at a glance. That is a genuine service, and I am not an enemy of charts; I make them weekly. But the translation has a property you must never forget: the eye believes the geometry before the mind reads the numbers. If the geometry exaggerates, the reader feels the exaggeration as fact and may never consult the digits at all. Every leaning technique in this lesson works through that one property. The numbers stay honest. The geometry lies on their behalf.

The first and most common lean is the cut axis. An axis is the numbered line along the bottom or the side of a chart that gives the scale. In a bar chart, each bar's length stands for its value, and the eye compares lengths. That comparison is only honest if the axis starts at zero, because a bar's length is measured from where the axis begins. Suppose our business's monthly enquiries run like this: ninety-six, ninety-eight, one hundred, and one hundred and two across four months — a gentle rise of six, across the whole period, on a base near one hundred. Drawn from zero, the four bars stand nearly equal, which is the truth: stability with a slight improvement. Now cut the axis: start it at ninety. The visible bars are now proportional to six, eight, ten, and twelve, and the last bar stands twice as tall as the first. The eye reports a doubling. The numbers report a rise of about six percent. Both charts use identical data. One of them is a lie told in lengths. When you meet a bar chart, your first glance belongs not to the bars but to the axis: where does it start? If it does not start at zero, the bars cannot be trusted as lengths, and you must read the numbers and ignore your eyes, which will object. Let them object. You are in charge.

A qualification, because exactness is our religion here: for line charts, which show change over time as a path rather than as bars, a non-zero start is sometimes defensible — a temperature chart that began at absolute zero would show nothing at all. The sin is not the cut itself. The sin is the cut without notice, in a chart whose visual force depends on the reader assuming a full scale. The honest remedies are simple: start at zero, or mark the break in the axis visibly, or choose a form that does not trade on length. A chart-maker who cuts an axis and hides the cut has told you something about themselves that no subsequent chart from the same hand should make you forget.

The second lean is the cherry-picked range. A range, here, is the stretch of time or the set of cases the chart includes. Every chart must include something and exclude something else; choosing is unavoidable. Leaning begins when the choice is made by the conclusion — when the maker tries start dates and end dates until the picture agrees with the sentence they intend to say, and then publishes that picture as if it were the whole story. Our business's revenue, by month, rises and falls with the seasons, as lesson four established. A chart from November to January shows a glorious climb. A chart from January to March shows a depressing slide. A chart of the full two years shows a wavy line, roughly level, with winters on top — the truth, which is less exciting than either excerpt and more useful than both. When a chart shows you a range, ask what lies immediately outside it, on both sides. The data just outside the frame is the data the maker decided you did not need. Decide for yourself whether they were right. Usually the question answers itself the moment it is asked out loud.

The third lean you already own from lesson one: the missing denominator. A chart of counts — complaints doubled, incidents soared — that never tells you out of how many. Complaints rising from five to ten is a doubling. If customers rose in the same period from five hundred to two thousand, then the complaint rate — complaints per customer — actually fell by half: five over five hundred is one percent; ten over two thousand is zero point five percent. The count doubled. The rate halved. The chart of counts, alone, announces a crisis in a business that is, by the rate, improving. Rates need denominators, and charts that show counts where rates are the honest measure are leaning, whether or not the maker intended to lean. Intent is not the standard in this class. Effect is. A chart that reliably misleads the reasonable reader is a leaning chart, full stop, and the maker's pure heart does not straighten it.

The fourth lean is the stretched picture: the same chart drawn tall and narrow to make a rise look steep, or short and wide to make the same rise look flat. The numbers and even the axis can be impeccable while the proportions do the persuading. There is no single correct proportion for a chart, which is exactly why the choice is a rhetorical one. The defence is the habit you now have: read the numbers at the ends of the line before admiring the slope. A rise from one hundred to one hundred and two is a rise of two percent, at any steepness, in any font, in any colour. Slope is theatre. Endpoints are data.

Fifth, the three-dimensional decoration and its cousins: bars drawn as cylinders, pies tilted toward the viewer, icons scaled by height when their area does the visual work. If an icon doubles in height and also doubles in width, its area quadruples, and the eye reads the area. A chart that doubles the picture's area for a doubling of the number has exaggerated by a factor of two without touching a digit. Pie charts deserve a special note. A pie chart shows parts of a whole as slices. Used for a few parts that genuinely sum to a whole — the sixty predictions dividing into thirty-nine hits and twenty-one misses — a pie is honest and clear. Used for many slices, or for numbers that do not sum to anything, it becomes a coloured puzzle in which the eye cannot rank the slices it most needs to compare. Bars rank. Pies decorate. Choose accordingly.

Now this class's set problem, which I will work in full, as is my custom. The problem: find one chart — anywhere — that leans: a cut axis, a cherry-picked range, a missing denominator. Describe in three sentences what it wants you to believe and what it hides. The worked answer is a method, not a chart: name the claim, then ask three questions — what is the denominator, what range was chosen and what was left outside it, and does the axis start where honesty starts? A chart that survives all three has earned your belief; one that fails any has told you what it is. Practise the method on this example with me. A software company advertises: customer complaints cut in half since our tool launched. Its chart shows monthly complaints falling from forty in March to twenty in June, bars drawn from an axis that starts at zero — good — across exactly those four months. Run the questions. Denominator: absent. The company's customer count is nowhere on the chart; if customers also halved in those months, the rate never moved. Range: March to June. What lies outside? July, in which complaints, let us suppose, returned to thirty-eight — outside the frame, where inconvenient months live. Axis: honest. Verdict: one pass, two failures. The chart wants you to believe the tool halved dissatisfaction. What it hides is the base the complaints came from, and the month that undid the story. Three sentences. That is the worked answer, and it is now yours to reuse on every chart anyone shows you, including — especially — charts made by people you like.

Here is your guided moment. Think of the last chart that persuaded you of something — in a meeting, in the news, in an advertisement you half-remember. Rebuild it in your mind and run the three questions slowly. Denominator: can you state it? If you cannot, the chart never gave it to you, and you were persuaded without it. Range: what would the months or cases just outside do to the picture? Axis: where did it start, and did you check at the time, or did the bars simply look the way they looked? Most people, doing this honestly, discover that the chart that persuaded them would fail at least one question. That discovery is not an embarrassment. It is the lesson working. The next chart will meet a different reader.

What does an honest chart look like, positively? It states its denominator in the title or directly under it. It shows a range long enough to include the boring parts. Its axis starts at zero, or says loudly that it does not. Its proportions are calm. Its title states the finding the numbers support — not the finding the maker wishes they supported. And it prints hits and misses together when the subject is a record: our business's predictions chart, done honestly, is sixty columns or one line with all sixty points, thirty-nine hits and twenty-one misses in the same colours of dignity, the misses not greyed, not shrunk, not exiled to a footnote. A chart of only the hits would be the visual form of the lie from lesson one: every element accurate, the collection misleading. Geometry cannot rescue a dishonest selection, and an honest selection needs no rescue. The two virtues — honest selection, honest geometry — are the whole craft. Everything else is software.

One more species deserves naming before the recap: the chart with two vertical axes, one on each side, each with its own scale, letting two lines be made to cross, kiss, or diverge at the maker's pleasure by stretching either scale. Two-axis charts are not always dishonest, but they are always adjustable, and an adjustable picture is an argument wearing a lab coat. When you meet one, cover either line with your hand and ask what the other line alone, on its own scale, actually shows. Usually: less than the pair appeared to promise. Correlation by draughtsmanship is still not causation, as lesson four would remind the chart, if charts could blush.

Let me work a second chart completely, this one drawn from our own business, so you can watch an honest chart being built and a leaning one being repaired. Take the predictions record: sixty predictions across six months, ten per month, with hits per month of six, seven, five, eight, six, and seven. Add them: six plus seven is thirteen, plus five is eighteen, plus eight is twenty-six, plus six is thirty-two, plus seven is thirty-nine. Thirty-nine hits, twenty-one misses, as always. The leaning version of this chart shows only the best month — eight hits out of ten, eighty percent — under the title Our Record-Breaking Month. Every number is true. The chart is a cherry-pick in a frame: the range is one month, chosen by the conclusion, and the other fifty predictions are outside it, unmentioned. The honest version shows all six months as bars from zero, each bar labelled with its count out of ten, under a title that states the whole: Thirty-Nine Hits and Twenty-One Misses in Sixty Predictions. The honest chart is less thrilling. It is also the one you could defend in a room full of enemies, which is my working definition of a finished chart. Thrill is available elsewhere, cheaply. Defendability is the scarce good.

Notice, in that repair, what changed and what did not. No number changed. The range widened to the whole record, the denominator — sixty, and ten per month — moved onto the chart's face, and the title began stating the whole finding instead of its best fragment. Three repairs, all of them matters of selection and labelling rather than arithmetic. This is typical. Leaning charts are rarely arithmetic failures. They are framing decisions, made one at a time, each small enough to excuse, accumulating into a picture that argues far beyond its data. Which is why the audit must also proceed one decision at a time: axis, range, denominator, proportion, title. Five checks, in that order, take under a minute. I have timed it, in classrooms, with a stopwatch I do not entirely trust, which is why I say under a minute rather than a precise figure.

A word on colour, since charts arrive coloured and colour is never neutral. Colour directs the eye: the red bar is read as the problem, the green bar as the success, before any number is consulted. A maker can paint the competitor's bar red and their own green while the values differ by a hair, and the verdict will be absorbed as decoration. Colour can also carry honest information — hits in one consistent colour, misses in another, across every chart a business publishes, so a regular reader learns the code once and reads faster forever. The rule is the same as everywhere in this lesson: decoration that argues is leaning; decoration that labels is craft. Ask of every colour what work it is doing. If the answer is that it makes the smaller number look alarming, you have found the lean.

Truncation has a quieter sibling I should name: the dual trick of the broken time axis, where equal spaces on the page represent unequal stretches of time. Months march evenly — January, February, March — and then the chart quietly skips to September, keeping the spacing, so a slow six-month change reads as a sudden jump. The line looks continuous. The time is not. Check the labels along the bottom with the same suspicion you give the numbers along the side. A chart's honesty lives as much in its spacing as in its scale, and gaps in time that are not marked as gaps are ranges cherry-picked at the level of the ruler itself.

Now, fairness to chart-makers, because this lesson could leave you merely suspicious, and suspicion alone is a poor instrument. Charts compress. Compression always discards. A chart of ten years of daily data must summarise or become wallpaper, and every summary chooses. The honest maker is not the one who discards nothing — that maker is a table — but the one whose discards are visible, stated, and not chosen by the conclusion. Show the full range in small print beside the excerpt. State the denominator in the title. Mark the axis break. These courtesies cost the maker nothing but the lean itself, which is precisely why their absence is informative. A maker who will not state the denominator is telling you the denominator would not help the argument. Believe them.

Apply that standard, finally, to the charts our business itself publishes, because this class's standard applies at home first, as lesson four insisted. The predictions chart we repaired a moment ago is the template: whole record, denominators on its face, misses at full size. The advertising chart gets the same treatment: clicks and customers side by side, so the rate cannot hide behind the count, and the range long enough to include the season's turn. A business that publishes charts it could defend in a room full of enemies will occasionally publish a chart that disappoints it. That disappointment is the receipt proving the system works. The alternative — charts that never disappoint their maker — is not a communications strategy. It is a symptom, diagnosable from the charts alone, by the methods of this lesson, in under a minute per chart. I have timed that too. The stopwatch and I have agreed to disagree about the seconds; about the diagnosis, never.

One more lean, small and ubiquitous, deserves its thirty seconds: the percentage-point shuffle. When a rate moves from two percent to three percent, that is a rise of one percentage point, and also a rise of fifty percent relative to where it started. Both statements are true. They produce entirely different feelings, and chart titles choose between them by the feeling required. A maker wanting alarm says complaints up fifty percent. A maker wanting calm says complaints up one point. The defence is mechanical and by now familiar: reconstruct the two underlying rates, with their denominators, and the shuffle loses its power. One point, fifty percent — hold both, state both, and let no title choose your emotions for you. Feelings are yours. Titles are theirs. Keep the accounts separate.

And a closing observation about why leaning works at all, which returns us to the first paragraph. The eye is fast and the mind is lazy — not as an insult, but as engineering: visual comparison costs nothing, while reading axes and hunting denominators costs effort, and effort is rationed. Leaning charts are priced for the rationing. They are built for the reader who will not spend the minute. This lesson's entire ambition is to make you a reader who spends the minute — on charts that matter, where money or belief will move because of them. You cannot audit every chart that crosses your screen, and I do not ask it. Audit the ones that ask something of you. A chart that wants nothing from you may lean in peace. A chart that wants your money, your vote, or your signature gets the three questions, the five checks, and the full minute, every time, without apology to its maker.

A last distinction, because students reliably ask it: is a chart that leans the same as a chart that lies? Not quite, and the difference matters for how you respond. A lying chart states numbers that are false. It is rare, because false numbers are checkable and the checking ruins careers. A leaning chart states numbers that are true and arranges everything else — axis, range, base, proportion, colour, title — so the true numbers argue a conclusion they do not support. It is common, because arrangement is deniable in a way digits are not. Respond accordingly. To the lying chart: rejection. To the leaning chart: repair. Ask for the full range, the denominator, the axis from zero, and watch whether the conclusion survives its own data presented honestly. Sometimes it does, and then you have gained a finding as well as a chart. More often the conclusion quietly shrinks to fit the honest picture, and the shrinking is the information you were meant not to receive. Either way, you now hold the tools. The chart's maker had them first. That advantage is hereby cancelled.

One practical drill closes the teaching, because this lesson, more than any other in the class, is a skill of the eyes and skills are built by repetition. For one week, every chart you encounter that asks something of you gets one written line in a notebook: the claim, the denominator or its absence, the range or its suspicious edges, the axis and where it starts. One line, three facts, no essays. At the week's end, read your lines back. You will see the leans cluster — the same missing denominator, the same flattering quarter — because leaning is a craft with fashions, and once you have logged a fashion twice you will spot it the third time before the chart finishes loading. That is expertise, in this domain: not a degree, not a title, but a notebook of caught attempts and the reflex they built. The businesses and publications that lean are counting on your reflex being admiration. Give them a different one.

Recap, in order. One: a chart translates numbers into geometry, and the eye believes the geometry before the mind reads the numbers. Two: a cut axis on a bar chart makes small differences look enormous; check where the axis starts before trusting any bar's length. Three: a cherry-picked range shows the stretch that agrees with the conclusion; ask what lies just outside the frame. Four: counts without denominators lean; the rate may move opposite to the count. Five: proportion, decoration, and doubled icons exaggerate without touching a digit; read endpoints, not slopes. Six: the method for any chart is three questions — denominator, range, axis — and a chart that fails any one has told you what it is. Seven: the honest chart states its base, shows the boring parts, keeps its geometry calm, and prints hits and misses together.

Before the questions, do the homework-shaped thing once, here, with me, on a chart I invent for the purpose — because the set problem asks you to find a leaning chart anywhere, and I want your first attempt supervised. A gym advertises: membership doubled in a year. Its chart shows two bars, last January and this January, the second twice the first, axis from zero, clean proportions. Run the questions. Denominator: members out of what — the town, last year's members, the people who saw the advertisement? The chart does not say, and doubled membership from a base of nine is a different event from doubled membership from a base of nine hundred. Range: January to January. What lies outside? February, when the resolution crowd traditionally departs — the chart's chosen endpoints are the two most flattering dates in the fitness calendar, which is either a coincidence or a range chosen by its conclusion, and you may form your own view. Axis: passes. Verdict: the bars are honest and the argument leans, through base and range, without a single false number. Write that verdict in three sentences and you have done the set problem once, correctly. Do it again, out there, on a chart that was not built to be caught, and the method is yours for life.

Next, the questions on this lesson, with the full text open beside them. Going back to read is learning, not cheating. Take the three questions with you in their shortest form — denominator, range, axis — the way you took lesson one's three and lesson three's four. You will notice the sets rhyme: all of them ask what was counted, out of how many, over what stretch, and what was left outside the frame. That rhyme is not an accident of my teaching. It is the shape of honesty itself, which turns out to have very few moving parts, endlessly recombined. Learn the parts once and every new disguise the lean invents will still be wearing them, visible to you, nameable by you, in the minute the chart hoped you would not spend.

You have now audited charts as a reader. The final step of this lesson is to hold the standard as a maker, because you will make charts — in a report, in a pitch, in a message to a partner — and the minute you make one, every temptation catalogued today will present itself as a formatting choice. Resist at the level of the choice, not the intention: set the axis before you look at the picture it makes, fix the range before you know which range flatters, write the denominator into the title before you see whether the title still sings. Order is the whole defence. A maker who decides the frame before seeing the picture cannot cherry-pick, because the picking would have to be done blind. That is the predictions record's discipline, translated into geometry: commit first, look second, publish the whole. Do that, and your charts will occasionally argue against you in public, which is how your readers will learn — correctly — that when your charts argue for you, they can be believed.

In lesson six, the final lesson, the subject is your own data: who holds it, what it can prove, and what it cannot. Bring your curiosity, and bring the whole course with you — the questions, the tables, the margins, the confounders, and the three chart checks — because the last lesson assembles them around the data closest to you; the rest is provided.

lessons.title: Your own data: who holds it, and what it can prove
paragraphs: Good to see you. Today AI and Computing earns its keep. I am Professor Juhani Korhonen, and this is lesson six of six in Data — Where It Lives and What It Proves: your own data — who holds it, and what it can prove. For five lessons the data belonged to a small marketing business: its customer list, its advertising numbers, its predictions record. Today the subject is closer. You generate data every day — when you buy, when you search, when you move through the world with a phone in your pocket — and almost none of it lives with you. This lesson maps where it lives, who holds it, what it can honestly prove about you, and what it cannot prove, however confidently someone reads it. I write the units on the board before opinions, every time. Bring your curiosity; the rest is provided.

Begin with a definition you already own. Data is recorded observation. Your data is the recorded observations of you: what you bought, where you were, what you clicked, what you searched for, whom you called, and when. Each of those is a row in somebody's table — lesson two's rows and columns, with you as the case. A record of this kind has a holder: the person or organisation that keeps the table. The holder of your data is rarely you. The shop holds the record of the sale. The phone company holds the record of the call. The platform holds the record of the click. You were present for every one of these events. Presence is not possession. That sentence explains most of the modern world, and we will spend the lesson on its consequences.

Let us inventory one ordinary day, slowly, because the length of the list is itself the lesson. You wake and check the weather on your phone: a record exists of the request, the time, and roughly where the phone was. You buy coffee with a card: the card company and the coffee shop both hold a record — the amount, the time, the place. You drive to work past a camera that reads number plates: a record. You search for a symptom, a gift, a train time: the search company holds each query, in order, with the hour attached. You message a friend: the messaging service holds the fact of the message, its time, and its size, and depending on the service, its contents. You stream music in the evening: a record of every track, every skip, every pause. By midnight, the day has produced, conservatively, hundreds of recorded observations of you, held by perhaps a dozen organisations, in tables you will never see, under rules you did not write. I am not describing a conspiracy. I am describing bookkeeping. Bookkeeping at scale, about everyone, retained for years — but bookkeeping, with all of bookkeeping's ordinary virtues and ordinary risks.

Who holds it, then, in categories. First, the organisations you deal with directly: shops, banks, employers, doctors, schools, and the government offices that tax you and license you. Their records exist because a transaction or a duty required them, and they are usually the most accurate data about you in existence, because errors in them cause immediate trouble that somebody must fix. Second, the platforms: the search company, the social networks, the video and music services, the map on your phone. You pay these with attention and information rather than money, and their tables are the widest — not the deepest facts about any single event, but observations across your whole day and year. Third, the brokers. A data broker is a company whose business is buying, combining, and selling records about people it has never dealt with directly. You have no account with a broker. You cannot picture its office. It may nevertheless hold a file on you assembled from purchases, subscriptions, public records, and platform scraps — a table built entirely from other people's rows about you. Fourth, your own devices, which hold more than most people realise: the phone keeps its own logs, the browser keeps its history, the photos carry the time and often the place they were taken, written into the file itself. That last category is the only one where the holder is you, and it is larger than you think. We will return to it, because it is the foundation of the only practical advice this lesson gives.

Now combine the categories, because combination is where the power and the trouble both live. Separately, each holder knows a slice: the shop knows the purchase, the platform knows the search, the phone company knows the tower your phone spoke to. Combined — sold, shared, breached, or lawfully requested — the slices assemble into a pattern of life: where you live and work, when you sleep, what you buy, what worries you at three in the morning, whom you know. No single record says any of that. The pattern emerges from the joining of tables, exactly the operation lesson two taught you with customer numbers and order numbers, performed here with you as the key. A key, you will recall, is a field that identifies each row uniquely. Your name, your phone number, your email address, and the identifying numbers your devices broadcast serve as keys across other people's tables. That is why a breach at a company you barely remember joining can matter: it is rarely the slice that harms. It is the key, escaping, that lets your slices be joined by strangers.

So much for who holds it. Now the second half of the title: what can it prove? Apply the standards of this class, without favour, because the subject is you. Your data can prove transactions: that this card bought this item at this time in this place. Transaction records are strong data — recorded at the moment, by a rule, with money attached to their accuracy. Your data can prove presence, approximately: that this phone was near this tower, that this card was used in this town. Approximately is the operative word, and honest readers keep it attached. Your data can prove sequences: searches made in an order, purchases across a season, journeys between places. Sequences are where records become stories, and stories, as lesson four taught you, are where causation gets pasted onto correlation by interested speakers. Hold that thought; we will need it in two minutes.

Here is what your data cannot prove, and this list matters more. It cannot prove intent. A search records the query, not the reason for it: the same search is made by the worried, the curious, the novelist researching a character, and the student writing an essay. The record is identical. The intents are opposites. Anyone who reads a motive off a log is adding the motive themselves and billing the log for it. It cannot prove attention: a video playing is a record of a screen, not of eyes, still less of agreement. It cannot prove character. A person's records show what they did, in the places that keep records, under the circumstances that produced the records. The unrecorded remainder of a life — the kindnesses done in cash and in person, the thoughts never searched for, the visits never logged — does not appear, and its absence from the table is not evidence about its size. Survivorship's mirror image, from lesson one: the table shows the recorded, and the recorded is a biased sample of a life, biased toward the digital, the commercial, and the recent. Conclusions about a whole person drawn from their data commit the exact error lesson three named: treating a sample — a slanted, convenience sample — as the population.

The predictions record returns here, for the last time, as the contrast that clarifies everything. Our business's record could prove what it proved because it was made in advance, kept whole, and kept by the business itself, for its own questions. Your data, as held by others, fails each of those tests in instructive ways. It was not made for your questions; it was made for the holder's questions — billing, advertising, security — and it answers yours only incidentally, when it answers them at all. It is not kept whole for you: holders keep what serves them, delete what does not, and show you, at most, an edited view — a dashboard, a history page — which is a filtered view of the kind lesson two warned you never to mistake for the whole table. And it was not made in advance for the claims later built on it: a log assembled for billing will be read, years later, as if it were a diary, which it is not. A diary records what its writer meant to say. A log records what a system happened to notice. Reading a log as a diary is the characteristic data error of our time, committed daily by employers, insurers, journalists, and governments, in ascending order of consequence.

Let me give you the guided moment for this lesson, and it is a practical one. Take one service you use daily — the search company, the music service, the map. Find, after this lesson, the page where it shows you your history: nearly every platform has one, usually under words like activity, history, or your data. Read it as you have been trained to read. Ask lesson one's three questions of it. What exactly was observed — the query, or the reason for the query? How much is here, and over what period? And is this the whole record, or the part the holder chooses to display? Then ask lesson five's question: what would this page look like as a chart, and what would the chart hide? You will learn two things in ten minutes: how much of your life is written down in that one table, and how carefully the display has been arranged to feel smaller than the table. Both lessons are worth the ten minutes. Do not skip the second because the first is interesting.

What, then, can actually be done? This class deals in what is true, not in comfort, so the honest answer is: less than you would like, more than nothing, in a specific order. First, know that in many places the law gives you rights over your data — to see a copy of what a holder keeps about you, to correct what is wrong, and in some places to ask for deletion. The details differ by country and by state, they change, and I am a physicist, not a lawyer; treat that sentence as a direction to look, not as legal advice. The looking is worthwhile: a request for your own file is the one audit of other people's tables about you that the system itself provides for. Second, correct what is wrong where you find it. Your file at a broker or a bank is a table, and tables carry duplicates, stale addresses, and other people's rows merged into yours — lesson two's four diseases, with your name on the folder. A wrong row in a table used for decisions about credit, work, or insurance is not an abstraction. Third, reduce what you generate where the cost to you is low: the permission a new application does not need, the account created for a single purchase, the history that can be set to expire. Do this without theatre. You are adjusting a flow, not escaping a system; the system is also the ambulance dispatch and the bank fraud alert, and a lesson that taught you to fear all recording would be a worse lesson than this one.

Fourth — and this is the point I most want kept — keep your own records. The business in our examples survived its confident moments because it held its own table: the predictions record, written in advance, hits and misses together. The personal equivalent is modest and entirely within your power. Keep your own copies of the documents that matter: contracts, receipts for large purchases, correspondence about money and work, the records of your own qualifications and your own creative work, with dates. Keep them in a place you control, in formats you can open, with a copy somewhere else against fire and failure. When a dispute ever comes — about what was agreed, what was paid, what you made and when — the party with records does not argue from memory. Memory is a poor storage device; that was lesson one, and it was always, also, about you. Your own table, kept whole, is the only dataset about your life whose choosing, keeping, and completeness you control. It will never be the largest table about you. It can be the most honest one, and in the rooms where it matters, honest and whole beats large.

One more application of the class's tools, because your data will be summarised back to you, constantly, and the summaries deserve auditing. Platforms will show you your year in review: your top songs, your most visited places, your streaks and totals. These are charts from lesson five, drawn from samples from lesson three, wearing correlations from lesson four. The totals will be counts without denominators — hours listened, without the hours awake. The categories will be the holder's categories, chosen for the holder's purposes, flattering in the direction of continued use. Enjoy them as entertainment; they are often charming. Do not mistake them for a portrait. A portrait of you drawn from your data would include the gaps, the unrecorded rooms, the denominator of your whole lived time — and no holder has those rows, because you lived them off the record, which is the normal human condition and, on the evidence of this lesson, a healthy one.

Let me also state the limit in the other direction, symmetrically, as this class insists. Your data being incomplete does not make it useless, and its holders are not villains in a story I am selling you. The same records that can be misread as a diary also catch the fraudster using your card in another country, find the phone you lost, and prove — when you need it proved — that you were somewhere, that you paid, that you sent the message before the deadline. Data about you is evidence, and evidence serves whoever reads it carefully, including you. The skill this whole class has been building — ask what was observed, count the denominator, hunt the confounder, check the axis, demand the whole record — is the skill of reading evidence carefully. Turn it, finally, on the evidence about yourself, and you will be neither paranoid nor naive about it, which is the only defensible position I know.

A concrete case will hold all of this together. Suppose a person applies for a job, and the employer buys a report assembled by a broker. The report says the applicant was associated with an address in another state for two years, and the employer's reader infers instability — a story, pasted onto rows. The rows themselves say less: a name resembling the applicant's appeared on a subscription at that address, merged into this file by a key match on the name alone. Two people, one name, one merged table — lesson two's duplicate disease, at national scale, with a person's livelihood as the stakes. The applicant who has kept their own records — leases, tax letters, dated correspondence — can do in one afternoon what no amount of confident arguing can do: put a whole, dated, first-party table next to the broker's assembled one and let the two be compared. That comparison, cross-checking, was the cheapest audit in existence when the subject was customers. It remains so when the subject is you. The moral is not that brokers always err. It is that their tables err at the ordinary rate of tables, and the correction mechanism is a better-kept table, held by the one person whose interest in its accuracy never sleeps.

Consider, too, the data you generate inside our own running example, because the marketing business holds data about its customers exactly as platforms hold data about you, and the symmetry is instructive. Its customer list is eight hundred rows of other people's data: names, addresses, first purchases. Its predictions record is about itself. The customers on that list have, most of them, never seen it, never corrected it, and would find in it the same diseases you would find in a broker's file on you — the forty ghosts, the stale addresses, the merged names. I do not tell you this to indict the business; its table is better kept than most, because its owner took lesson two. I tell you it so that the lesson's direction reverses cleanly in your mind: every table you keep about others deserves the care you wish holders would take with the tables they keep about you. The ethics of data, in this class, is not a separate subject. It is the same standard, applied in both directions — keep it whole, keep it accurate, show the person their rows when they ask, and never read a log as a diary, about a customer any more than about yourself.

One more distinction belongs in this final lesson, between data about you and data from you. Data from you is what you deliberately publish: the photograph you post, the comment you write, the review you sign. You chose its content, if not always its audience or its lifespan — a distinction worth a pause, because a post made for fifty friends and kept for fifteen years, searchable by employers and strangers, has changed its meaning without changing a word. Data about you is everything else in this lesson: the logs, the transactions, the inferences. Inferences deserve their own sentence, because they are the newest layer and the least visible. An inference is a conclusion a holder's system draws about you from your records: a category you are sorted into, a likelihood attached to your name — likely to move, likely to buy, likely to leave. Inferences are not observations. They are the holder's correlations, from lesson four, computed over millions of other people's rows and applied to yours, confounders unhunted, mechanisms unstated. Your file increasingly consists of them. When a decision about you is made from your file, the part that decided it may be neither a fact nor a record, but a resemblance — you pattern-match people who behaved a certain way. Knowing that resemblance is not evidence, and that you are entitled in many places to ask which of the two decided your case, is the grown-up form of everything this class has taught.

And a last word on deletion, because it is the promise most often made about your data and the one most loosely kept. Deleting a record from the table you can see — the history page, the account, the application — removes that view. Whether it removes the holder's underlying rows, the copies already sold or shared, the backups, and the inferences already drawn from it, are four further questions, and the answers are usually four different answers. This is not an accusation; backups and fraud records have honest reasons to persist. It is a calibration. The delete button is a real tool with a smaller radius than its label suggests, and a person who understands tables will use it where it helps, without believing it reaches the brokers, the backups, and the already-drawn conclusions. Precision about what a tool does is the beginning of using it well. That sentence, you may notice, could stand as the motto of all six lessons, and I will not pretend the resemblance is accidental.

One worked miniature, with numbers, before we close — because this class trusts arithmetic more than adjectives, including on the subject of you. A fitness application on your phone records your steps. On Tuesday it reports eight thousand four hundred steps; on Wednesday, nine thousand one hundred. A summary, later, announces your most active day and builds a small chart of your week, bars rising proudly. Audit it with the tools you now own. What was observed? Not steps, exactly: the phone observed accelerations, and an algorithm counted some of them as steps — a metric, lesson one, standing for the thing it names. The denominator: the chart shows the days the phone was carried, charged, and awake; the day you left it on the dresser is absent from the table, not recorded as zero — an empty field, lesson two, silently dropped from the average. The sample: your carried days stand for your life the way Saturday shoppers stood for all customers in lesson three, which is to say, imperfectly and in a known direction. The correlation the summary implies — that you were more virtuous on Wednesday — has confounders: Wednesday was the day you paced during a long call and twice walked to the shop you drove to on Tuesday. None of this makes the record useless. Eight thousand four hundred counted accelerations is a real observation, useful for comparing like with like. It makes the record a record — of a phone, an algorithm, and a carried week — rather than a verdict on a person. That demotion, from verdict to record, is the single most valuable move in this entire lesson, and it generalises to every file, report, and summary about you that you will ever be shown. Demote first. Then decide what the demoted thing is actually worth, which is sometimes a great deal, and never everything.

Recap, in order. One: your data is the recorded observations of you, held mostly by others — presence is not possession. Two: the holders fall into kinds — the organisations you deal with, the platforms, the brokers who assemble files without ever meeting you, and your own devices, the one category you hold yourself. Three: slices join into a pattern of life through keys — your name, number, and addresses are the fields that let tables about you be combined. Four: your data can prove transactions, approximate presence, and sequences; it cannot prove intent, attention, or character. Five: a log is not a diary — records made for billing and advertising answer your questions only incidentally, and the view a holder shows you is a filtered view, not the whole table. Six: your practical defences are to use your rights to see and correct your files, to reduce what you generate where the cost is low, and above all to keep your own records, whole, in a place you control.

If you take one practical hour from this lesson, spend it like this. Twenty minutes: open the activity pages of the two or three services you use most, and read them with the three questions, noting — actually noting, in writing — what was observed, what period the record covers, and whether what you are shown claims to be the whole table or a view of it. Twenty minutes: gather your own documents that matter into one place you control, with a copy elsewhere — the contracts, the receipts, the certificates, the dated record of work that is yours. Twenty minutes: correct one wrong thing somewhere — the stale address, the merged name, the permission an application never needed. An hour, three tasks, no purchases, no new accounts, no applications to install. At the end of it you will not have escaped the system, which was never the offer. You will have done something rarer and more useful: you will have looked at your own data with the same exactness you now bring to everyone else's claims, and acted on what you saw at the scale where action is actually possible. That is what this class means by literacy. Not suspicion. Not innocence. Inspection, followed by proportionate action, recorded — of course — in a table of your own.

That is the end of the teaching, and the end of the class. Six lessons: what data is, where it lives, how some can stand for all, why together is not because, how pictures lean, and whose hands your own rows rest in. You came in, most likely, believing that data was something other people had and other people argued about. You leave knowing it is a practice: observe honestly, record in advance, keep it whole, state the denominator, price every claim at the strength its design has earned. Do that, in a business or in a life, and you will be lied to measurably less often, including — especially — by yourself. Next, the questions on this lesson, with the full text open beside them. Going back to read is learning, not cheating; it was never cheating, in any lesson, and it is a good habit to end on. Bring your curiosity to whatever you study next; the rest, as ever, is provided. It has been a pleasure to teach you. I mean that precisely, which is the only way I mean anything. The units are off the board now, all six of them, in order, as promised on the first day: what counts, where it lives, how some stands for all, why together is not because, how pictures lean, and who holds your rows. Keep the board in your head. It fits. That was always the design, from the first definition to this last inventory of your own rows, held in other people's tables and, from today, a little more firmly in your own.
